records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 223/04/2026 The food-at-home pressure: A key driver of recent inflation dynamics and our 2027 upward revision is the sharp rise in producer prices, especially in agricultural components. Agricultural producer prices (IPA, part of the PPI) have shown a steady upward trend – a 2.44% rise in March – signalling strong pipeline pressure. Three main factors explain it: Energy and logistics costs: Geopolitical tension in the Middle East has lifted oil prices, which feed freight costs, distribution margins and, consequently, farm-production costs. Because Brazil relies on road transport, the diesel- to-food price pass-through is rapid and sizable. Global commodity prices: Not only oil but also agricultural commodities have rebounded, buoyed by recent trade disruptions, higher input costs and supply uncertainty. This flips the late-2025 trend, when food prices pulled inflation down. Fertiliser risks: A structural concern is fertiliser supply. We expect potential disruptions from the geopolitical tension and medium-term fallout from the conflict. Because Brazil’s 2026–2027 planting window is August- September, costs will rise and harvests may shrink, meaning food-price pressure could linger into 2027 and extend beyond the current shock. records.text: M Idea 8 Rates Strategy: A Nuanced Set-up for the Front-End Fabio Bassanin We have limited conviction on the market reaction to the April MPC, as the price action will depend not only on the headline decision, but also on the framing of the scenarios, the signal from the policy rules, the eventual vote split and the tone of the individual paragraphs. Our base case remains a hawkish hold, with an 8:1 split and Pill voting for a hike. On the messaging, we expect a somewhat more balanced tone than in March, with the opening paragraphs of the minutes likely to emphasise the high degree of uncertainty around the outlook. That said, the BoE could still retain a tightening bias, linked to a judgement that the risks of second-round effects are rising, rather than to evidence that such effects have already emerged. The market reaction will therefore depend on which element dominates. If markets focus primarily on the inflation risks, front-end rates could remain priced for a significant degree of further tightening. If greater weight is placed on the growth trade-off, the response could prove more supportive for duration. More broadly, the framing of the scenarios, the vote split and the lean in the individual paragraphs could tilt the market reaction in either direction. That said, the hawkish market reaction to the March MPC may itself argue for a more carefully balanced tone this time around. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 17 United Kingdom Data in the UK continues to be somewhat resilient but the trajectory points to weaker growth and higher inflation. GDP growth is robust at a headline level but the composition leaves us cautious about over-interpreting the strength, particularly as manufacturing growth already looks weak going into the energy shock. Official data for March is not yet available. We expect to see a significant jump in non-core inflation in March which will likely keep CPI between 3.0-3.3% through the remainder of the year. As of yet, there is little suggestion that second-round effects will be as severe as they were in 2022/23 with initial wage projections not reacting and leading indicators for food still relatively calm. That said, we expect the BoE to remain cautious, particularly given the volatility in inflation expectations. We continue to see the BoE on hold through the rest of 2026. The cyclical position of the UK, with labour market slack still building and GDP running below potential, in combination with a still restrictive policy rate already appears to be weighing on prices. records.text: Global Asset Allocation 24 April 2026 Citi Research 15 ECB stuck between a rock and a hard place: neutral Bunds. Out of the three main central banks in G10 outside of Japan, the ECB is probably the most likely to respond to the energy shock with price hikes, at least in the near term. Both the BoE and the Fed were in the middle of their slow-paced and data dependent cutting cycle when the war broke out. As the war began markets aggressively priced hikes in all three, particularly in the UK, likely as a result of stretched received positioning in the UK front-end. But after the first round of central banks meetings, BoE governor Bailey was quick to adjust the narrative and calm markets, pointing out that markets are getting ahead of themselves pricing in hikes (Reuters, 1 April). For the Fed new chair Warsh is likely to continue to support cuts according to our economists. The ECB instead was already at neutral when the conflict began, and a prolonged conflict is likely to trigger a reaction, which could come as early as Jun / July. As our strategists put it, the ECB in particular faces two-way credibility risks. Act too early and risk policy error via lower growth, or too late and risk policy error with higher inflation. While the bias of top officials seems to be to accept growth risks and possibly hike early, we think it is still hard to position for hikes in Bunds. records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 April 2026 Citi Research 8 We look at the relationship between a naïve carry strategy on € 10s30s and implied vol over a three-month horizon. We find that the relationship between vol and curve carry is not only asymmetric (negative when vol goes up, but nearly flat otherwise) and non-linear (depending on the level of implied vol). From higher vol to flatter 10s30s. The (negative) relationship between carry strategies and volatility is well documented: intuitively, when uncertainty about the “active” part of a fixed-income asset (the change in PV coming from future moves in its discount / yield curve) increases, the PnL contribution from the current difference between forward and spot rate becomes less relevant. More interesting is the stylized fact that the relationship between (i) the 3m PnL from a carry strategy deployed on € 10s30s and (ii) implied volatility (we take the 3m change in 3m implied vol, averaged across 2y and 10y tails) has really been negative only in the quadrant corresponding to higher vol / flatter curve (Figure 12). In other words, while it’s been the case that higher vol has been met by a flatter 10s30s curve, there’s been an economically limited impact from higher vol on curve. Figure 12. records.text: Net Upside Risks to Our Price Forecasts Net Upside Risks to Crude Prices We illustrate the two-sided risks to our price forecasts, which tilt to the upside, with 3 risk scenarios (Exhibit 1): Adverse scenario: Brent 2026Q4 would average just over $100 assuming Gulf n exports only normalize from mid-June through end-July (and 0.5mb/d of scarring to Gulf capacity, as in baseline). Severely adverse scenario: Brent 2026Q4 would average at nearly $120 assuming n Gulf exports normalize from mid-June through end-July and 2.5mb/d of scarring to Gulf capacity. This 2.5mb/d of scarring is equivalent to flows through the Strait not recovering above 70% (till pipeline capacity is expanded). Benign scenario: Brent 2026Q4 would average just under $80 assuming Gulf n exports normalize from early May to mid-June, no Gulf production scarring, and stronger supply responses from the US and core OPEC. We see upside risk to estimated prices in the adverse and severely adverse scenarios because oil inventories are likely to reach very low levels, triggering non-linear price increases. Global visible total oil inventories are likely to reach the lowest level on record since 2018 (when satellite data started tracking global crude stocks) even in the benign scenario (Exhibit 11). records.text: M Update 2 Japan-Style Core CPI YoY Set to Accelerate Ahead: Mar 2026 Nationwide CPI Upside surprise of 0.1ppt driven by price hikes in selected household appliances: Japan- style core CPI (excluding fresh food) for March at the national level remained below 2% for a second consecutive month, but picked up to +1.8% YoY from +1.6% YoY in February ( Exhibit 1 ). This was 0.1ppt above our latest forecast. In addition to a larger positive contribution from energy items amid rising gasoline and kerosene prices linked to Middle East tensions, price increases for household durable goods were somewhat stronger at the national level than those already reported for the Tokyo preliminary CPI in March. In particular, price revisions were notable for household appliances such as room air conditioners (+11.0% MoM) and refrigerators (+17.2% MoM). While yen depreciation may be starting to feed through to prices for some appliances, for room air conditioners manufacturers may also be setting relatively aggressive prices in connection with model changes, anticipating replacement demand ahead of the tightening of energy-efficiency standards scheduled for April 2027. By contrast, among food-related items, price momentum continues to decelerate across many categories, led by rice, where inventories have been accumulating. The ECB wage tracker for 2026 was revised 0.1%-pt lower after the March meeting to a target-consistent level of 2.6%oya due to lower recent pay deals. Source: Zillow, Macrobond, Barclays Research What should we make of this? First, it is far from obvious that we should shift the baseline expectation to a permanent new run rate consistent with something like 5bp/month for ZORI, especially given the fundamentally different nature of what CPI shelter and Zillow rents measure. Instead, we see this development as warranting a higher weight placed on downside risks to the path of rent inflation. While eventually lower rent growth should translate into reduced supply and upward pressure on forward rents, in the meantime over a more forecastable horizon, the left tail is fattening. To see the consequences for headline CPI, we can consider a more holistic view for the risks to inflation persistence in 2027 from a run-rate lens ( Figure 3). If we start by assuming that rent of primary residence and OER run at something like 2.0% (in between the current baseline of ~2.5% and the pure 'downside scenario' noted above), then even if... • Core services ex RPR/OER holds at the current pace of ~3%• • Core goods rises at 60bp y/y (consistent with Barclays' baseline assumption of 5bp per• month) • Food rises 1pp above the long-run average• • Energy is flat in 2027 (despite the WTI curve implying 8% deflation)• ...then the resulting core is only at 2.0% and headline at 2.14%. On a cross-market basis, we recommend buying Sep26 SONIA calls versus Euribor. At the margin, we continue to expect fewer BoE hikes relative to ECB hikes in the euro area, the ECB's hawkish hold and staff projections flag clearer upside risks to medium-term infla- tion — including potential second-round effects — leaving our baseline centered on two 25bp hikes in 2026, in June and September. In contrast, recent BoE communication has leaned decidedly more cautious, with Governor Bailey explicitly seeking to dampen market tightening expectations while emphasizing the need to minimize damage to activity and employment. This has prompted us to revise our UK baseline down to a single 25bp hike in June, versus two hikes previously. Taken together, the bar for ECB tightening remains materially lower than for the BoE, implying a shallower UK hiking profile relative to the euro area over the course of 2026. The big acceleration in input and output prices is concerning and would give weight to the arguments of the hawks for the MPC to focus more decisively on price concerns. Household short term inflation expectations showed a record rise from 3.3% to 5.4% in March, highest since 2023 and long-term expectations rose from 3.6% to 4.5%, according to YouGov/Citi. While the key would be if this jump is sustained, it is something to be concerned about. The March Decision Maker Panel showed that firms' year ahead own price growth expectations rose from 3.4% to 3.7% and one year ahead inflation expectations jumped from 3.0% to 3.5% the biggest monthly jump since September 2022. On the dovish side, private wage continued to soften to 3.2%, below BoE’s forecast of 3.5% and payrolls showed a mild fall in March post conflict. Oil prices are similar and gas prices are somewhat lower vs. 16 March prices which the BoE referenced in the March meeting to give tentative inflation forecasts.

records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 April 2026 Citi Research 3 Negative 2yr real yields could become a problem for the ECB: The reasons why the ECB would respond to a large and persistent inflation deviation, “regardless of its origin”, has been set out via four channels by Chief Economist Lane (see 3 December): (1) cost-of-living impacts influencing subsequent price and wage setting; (2) real yield moves amplifying the inflation shock; (3) inflation expectations; (4) communication risk if there is no policy response. The real yield channel may already be in play. As Figure 2 shows, the 1yr € real yield has fallen to around -100bp and the 2yr real yield is about -30bp. A growing concern for the ECB might be that negative real yields over the policy relevant horizon could amplify inflationary pressures. Admittedly, there was no sign of this in the deliberations in March (see ECB Accounts, Mar26). Beyond the 5yr point, € real yields have risen since the conflict started. Indeed, they are historically elevated in 10yr space. New house view looks for 2x 25bp hikes, most likely in June and July: While it is a close call, our economics team now expect the ECB to follow through with hikes (see Global Economic Outlook & Strategy:Turmoil in the Middle East—Assessing the Longer-term Implications). The house view then looks for a long pause at 2.5%. On the one hand, demand destruction may prevent a fuller hiking cycle. On the other, wider fiscal stimulus may prevent the hikes being reversed. records.text: JGB transaction data: March sees further slowdown in JGB investment This section in an extract from Japan Flow Update: JGB transaction data: March sees further slowdown in JGB investment, 20 April. Please refer to the original report for a detailed analysis. March saw JGB investment slow further to JPY4.4trn from JPY6.2trn in February as buying by trusts and foreigners moderated amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. By maturity, net buying of superlong JGBs remained above JPY1.0trn for a fifth consecutive month despite slowing from the previous month as foreigners and trusts reduced their buying while insurers scaled back their selling. In long-term JGBs, on the other hand, foreign investors swung to a sizable net sale from the previous month, and with other investor types broadly flat, net buying fell to the JPY0.4trn range, near the level seen last September. While the size remains uncertain at this stage, (1) the fact that an extraordinary Diet session is typically convened in autumn to pass a supplementary budget, and (2) the assumption that funding for energy subsidies is secured through end-2026, together suggest that the scale of any supplementary budget compiled ahead of summer could amount to around ¥3–5tn. If crude oil prices were to fall sharply over the next one to two months, or if the government were to raise the ¥170/liter price cap and thereby scale back the size of gasoline subsidies, the risk of a pre-summer supplementary budget—and the size of such a budget—would diminish. However, given current Middle East developments and the government’s policy stance, we view both as facing high hurdles. Under the scheme, the government fully absorbs, via subsidies, the portion of the nationwide average retail gasoline price that exceeds ¥170/liter. At present, with subsidies of around ¥35/liter, retail gasoline prices have been capped at around ¥170/liter (Exhibit 1). This is lower than both pre-abolition levels of the provisional gasoline tax at end-2025 and prices seen at the same time last year. Given that Japan relies on the Middle East for more than 90% of its crude oil imports, gasoline (and other fuel oil products) is typically the category through which consumers are most quickly exposed to rising energy prices. However, the government’s de facto price cap should limit the near‑term inflationary impact of higher crude oil prices and help contain the negative effects on domestic consumption and growth. The trade-off is a continued rise in fiscal costs. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has indicated that maintaining subsidies of ¥30/liter for one month would entail fiscal costs of around ¥300bn. Hiking to 2.5% can be seen as still within the neutral range. The house view then looks for a long pause at 2.5%. On the one hand, demand destruction may prevent a fuller hiking cycle. On the other, wider fiscal stimulus may prevent the hikes being reversed. As such, this pushes up on our yield forecasts for the next couple of quarters – especially in the front-end – but only to a little above current market levels (which, at the time of writing, has retreated from fully priced 2x25bp). That gives a slight near-term bearish bias, forecasting 10yr Bunds to average 3.05% in 2Q26. In terms of the near-term trajectory for core goods, the US economics’ baseline forecast sees a 0.23% print in March, followed by about 14bps per month in Q2, and roughly 0% per month over Q3, Q4 and 2027 Q1. With more normal goods prints as tariffs roll off, the CPI -PCE wedge should normalize in early 2027 as base effects drop off. Risks to that view, however, do depend on whether the strong prints that we have seen in the smaller CPI categories persists. In particular, near-term momentum in computer software and accessory prices appears to remain strong. To the extent that inflation remains elevated in those categories, then the inverted CPI -PCE wedge could persist for longer. To the extent that there is negative payback in the next couple months, then this would help to normalize that wedge sooner. records.text: FX’s beta to nominal rate differentials is typically lower in supply shocks Real rather than nominal rate differentials have held greater relevance for EUR/USD since March, but under which environments is this generally the case? We argue this question can essentially be reduced to whether a widening in inflation differentials (i.e. a shift higher in domestic vs foreign inflation pricing) is currency-positive or currency-negative. Leveraging the San Francisco Fed’s decomposition of headline PCE inflation into supply and demand drivers, we find that demand-led inflation regimes typically produce a positive relationship between EUR/USD and EU-US inflation differentials (with a full-sample beta of +0.54), while this relationship is closer to neutral under supply-led inflation regimes (with a beta of +0.17) (Exhibit 5). Intuitively, we think this aligns with the notion that higher domestic inflation pricing can either represent firmer domestic aggregate demand (a currency-positive) or either lower supply or higher inflation premium/uncertainty (both of which are typically currency-negatives), and the different prevailing regimes help to identify which of these dynamics is dominating. EUR/USD’s declining beta to inflation differentials (and hence to nominal rate differentials) in the currency energy-driven supply shock is consistent with that broader finding. Over the past week, BEI fell from 5.65% to 5.39%, while Focus inflation 12 months ahead increases from 4.05% to 4.11%. As a result, the BEI-Focus gap narrowed meaningfully, from 1.60pp to 1.28pp. Despite the compression, the spread remains elevated, indicating that markets still price a relevant upside inflation risk premium. What happened this week: El Niño concerns The week brought news that may still pressure inflation expectations over the next 12 months. First, El Niño projections worsened, reinforcing medium‑term risks to food inflation, likely with lags extending into 2027. Second, last Friday was a critical Focus survey cutoff, and this Friday will be again, which may affect expectations amid incoming administered‑price decisions. Third, Aneel (National Electric Energy Agency) approved electricity tariff increases across several states, reinforcing energy‑related pressures during the next 12 months, adding fresh evidence that administered prices remain an active source of upside risk.

Per the release: "anecdotal evidence often cited growth tailwinds from technology investments...there were some reports of rising workloads due to data centre demand and higher defence spending in key export markets". The global themes of European rearmament and AI diffusion have been a strong tailwind to UK growth, with more lacklustre domestically-oriented sectors. Last month, for example, the ICT sector printed an Output PMI at ~55, compared to Tourism & Recreation at 35. The drop in the headline March data probably went a bit too far, and 52.0 seems a more accurate level to us – UK economy is growing at a modest pace, aided largely by global growth tailwinds. The sustainability of these, of course, does in large part depend on the news flow out of the Middle East, and the levels at which commodity prices will settle over the remainder of the year. The ONS growth data, we think, overstates the scale of acceleration in growth in 1Q, and, by extension, might understate the slowdown over 2Q/3Q. We are forecasting 0%Q growth on the ONS numbers, but see the "underlying growth pace" as closer to ~0.2%Q. All in all, however, there is little here to be alarmed about. Had the energy shock not materialised, the combination of less monetary policy restrictiveness and global tailwinds would have meant the UK would be positioned for a healthy, sustained acceleration over the coming year. Inflation jumped to 3.3% in March as expected, and despite slightly weaker core, services inflation rose to 4.5% (somewhat driven by airfares). This backdrop implies some hawkish risk going into next Wednesday’s Fed meeting, but we expect a mostly status-quo, “wait and see” stance for Powell’s (presumably) last meeting as Chair. Focus will be on any statement changes. We expect the language on job gains to change to “modest” from “low” reflecting the better March report. While not our base case, the risk is that the statement could include a reference to two-sided risk to future policy adjustments. Minutes from the last couple meetings have mentioned “some participants” supported this guidance. Chair Powell will likely acknowledge that labor market data have looked somewhat better and that risks to inflation remain. We still expect him to highlight that policy remains well positioned for the Fed to wait and see how data and the Middle East conflict evolve. GDP will likely rebound in Q1, we expect a 2.6% QoQ SAAR increase, boosted by the end of government shutdown and stronger investment, even as real consumption growth slows amid elevated consumer inflation. Core PCE inflation is expected to outpace core CPI again in March, up 0.29%MoM, reflecting strong core goods—boosted by software and computer accessories prices—moderate housing inflation, mixed non-housing services. T otal durable goods orders are likely to fall in March due to continued normalization of aircraft orders, but core durable goods orders should continue to be strong.

Views from JPMorganChase’s Chairman on Security Resilience and the American Dream Geopolitics is the big variable right now and this isn’t theoretical. The right approach isn’t to bet on one storyline, but to be ready for a wide range of outcomes. Modern conflicts don’t follow clean timelines—wars that “should” end quickly can drag on for years. And what’s happening today is bigger than normal headline risk; it can shape the strength of the broader democratic order in the face of revisionist powers and aligned disruptors. The point isn’t to sound overly optimistic or alarmist—it’s to think like a risk manager: map the range of plausible paths, accept that uncertainty is high, and make sure that operations can manage through each scenario. The goal is continuity and staying able to lend, clear, advise, invest, and support customers even when markets get stressed. The most dangerous moments are often psychological (e.g., when something breaks, everyone rushes for the exits, and the assumption of liquidity fails when you need it most). So instead of trying to predict the exact timing of shocks, build the capacity to absorb them. Resilience does not eliminate tipping points, and energy and security shocks can reprice rapidly, even if the underlying conflict ultimately moves toward a more stable endpoint. Growth likely to remain robust: We expect Malaysia's economic growth to remain robust, despite a slightly disappointing Q1 GDP advance estimate of 5.3% y/y (consensus: 5.5% y/y). Barring a rise in energy prices in a severe re-escalation, we believe investment, and exports will support full-year growth. Electronic exports will likely remain strong due to the resilience of the AI cycle, as seen by the strong export performance in the region. This should keep overall growth supported, given the supply chain linkages across the economy. On the investment front, data center investment will likely continue, while ongoing public infrastructure projects will also add to growth. Front-end MYR rates have been muted: Since the start of the conflict, front-end EM Asia rates have sold off in response to rising oil prices and inflation risks, with most of these moves partially retracing as oil prices peaked and then fell to current levels (Figure 1). We interpret current market pricing across the region as a combination of potential rate hike(s) if oil prices remain elevated and some risk premium in the front-end given the volatility of the Middle East situation. Malaysia stands out as an exception, however, with front-end swaps pricing in almost no chance of rate hikes (Figure 2). But with Gulf exports through the Strait still extremely low and the conflict unresolved, the benign route to a meaningful rally may not materialize swiftly. Meanwhile, the unwind of March FCI tightening likely leaves markets further away from an inflection point that would shift higher oil from an inflationary hawkish policy shock to a growth shock. That said, UST yield sensitivity to day-to-day oil fluctuations has declined (Exhibit 1), and we think the bar is high to test the sort of volatility seen early in the conflict given the higher starting level for yields and the role that positioning likely played in amplifying the more extreme March moves. With the Fed likely to retain its “wait and see” approach given inflation uncertainty and stability in the labor market data, the distance from a clear offramp leaves rate risks two-sided in the near term. That keeps the near-term bias towards finding ways to earn carry and insulating against the risk of higher inflation (more below) even as our medium-term views remain for lower yields. records.text: US Economics Weekly 24 April 2026 Citi Research 10 We expect total durable goods orders to decline again in March, falling by 1.9%MoM. This would reflect a continued normalization of aircraft orders, which have been very strong over the last year. Large aircraft orders could reflect foreign purchases of US-produced planes as part of various trade negotiations. While previous demand could keep activity in this sector supported, we would expect new demand for aircraft to slow in coming months, with higher input costs for airlines given the rise in jet fuel a new headwind. Excluding transportation goods, durable goods orders should remain strong, rising 0.5%MoM and with a 1.3% increase in core capital goods orders. This could reflect continued strong demand for AI-related goods like computers. Of course, higher energy and input costs could be a risk for continued strong industrial goods demand. Data like industrial production may be a better reflection of real activity trends in this sector, as durable goods orders are reported in nominal terms and may also be boosted by any price increases. Scandi | Swedish activity: After a quiet period in the Scandi, our focus next week will be on the 1Q26 Flash GDP on Wednesday. We expect the momentum to weaken to 0.2%Q, driven by weak household consumption and industrial activity in the first two months of the year. Government spending and exports should remain supportive. We think uncertainty from the Iran conflict and higher fuel prices will dampen the Monthly GDP for March and expect it at -0.1%M. In the Economic Tendency survey for April, we expect to see further deterioration in business and consumer sentiment. UK | BoE in focus: After a data-heavy week, the focus turns to the BoE. We expect an 8:1 vote for a hold, with Chief Economist Pill voting for a hike. Messaging-wise, it is hard to see anything but guidance of potential action should risks of second-round effects rise. Figure 13: Formula effect tightening may be structural Figure 14: Price dispersion likely to be the primary determinant of the magnitude of the formula effect Source: Deutsche Bank Research, Haver Analytics Source: Deutsche Bank Research, Haver Analytics This is relevant for inflation market valuations. Assuming the Fed maintains PCE inflation at 2% over time, the long-term fair value estimate for CPI inflation should now arguably be ~5bp lower than pre-2023. Weight differences expected to normalise over the next year As detailed in the US econ team’s recent outlook update (see “Outlook update: The (oil) drumbeat of war“ for more details), the main drivers of their inflation outlook are core goods eventually rolling over as tariff effects pass through and base effects roll off, modest further disinflation from housing, but super core inflation remaining sticky. Under thei r baseline forecasts, they see core CPI and core PCE ending the year around 2.7% and 2.9% (Q4/Q4) respectively, before ending 2027 with a more normal wedge: 2.6% and 2.3% (Q4/Q4). records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General INFLATION WORRIES We are now 5 years removed from the end of the pandemic, yet inflation in the US is still not back to target. The Fed’s initial year+ of restrictive rate policy was complicated by monetary quantity policy as they worked to balance their dual mandate. Chair Powell, as of this week, still does not believe that there is a strong relationship between monetary quantity and inflation, which helps explain the Fed’s actions. Whether he is right or not, we do know for sure that despite higher rates, nominal growth remains solid, the labor market remains relatively robust, and even if goods and services inflation has come down, disinflation had ended long before the Iran invasion began, asset inflation has been a persistent characteristic of the post pandemic world. Figure 3 Very little progress on getting inflation to target in the past 2 years Source: State Street Markets, BLS I have argued in previous papers that the Fed’s twice aborted bias to bring rates lower was premature, and the data backs this up. The Fed achieved steady disinflation during the restrictive period, and this progress was halted and reversed as the pause and cutting cycles began. In fact the Fed was left with an ideal situation, the labor market remained at historically stron g levels even during the move to restrictive policy, affording them the ability to maintain higher rates for longer and return price ap preciation to target. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 6 Consistent with our narrative, markets continue to see the Federal Reserve, the ECB, the Bank of England, and the RBA all pursuing tighter monetary policy paths as a result of the recent upsurge in oil prices and the accompanying inflation pressures (Figure 7). That said, these paths are notably less aggressive than a few weeks ago, when the situation looked more challenging. Only expectations for the Bank of Japan have remained stable through this period, with the markets continuing to expect a gradual normalization. In sync with the markets, we have raised our forecasts for monetary policy in 14 of the 27 major central banks that we follow, including many in both EM and DM economies (Figure 8). Notably, we now see the ECB hiking twice this year; we have concerns about the advisability of these hikes, but they strike us as likely. In contrast, our US team continues to believe that the Fed will look through the oil shock and ultimately cut rates later this year. Figure 7. records.text: US Economics Weekly 24 April 2026 Citi Research 10 We expect total durable goods orders to decline again in March, falling by 1.9%MoM. This would reflect a continued normalization of aircraft orders, which have been very strong over the last year. Large aircraft orders could reflect foreign purchases of US-produced planes as part of various trade negotiations. While previous demand could keep activity in this sector supported, we would expect new demand for aircraft to slow in coming months, with higher input costs for airlines given the rise in jet fuel a new headwind. Excluding transportation goods, durable goods orders should remain strong, rising 0.5%MoM and with a 1.3% increase in core capital goods orders. This could reflect continued strong demand for AI-related goods like computers. Of course, higher energy and input costs could be a risk for continued strong industrial goods demand. Data like industrial production may be a better reflection of real activity trends in this sector, as durable goods orders are reported in nominal terms and may also be boosted by any price increases. records.text: US Policy Risks While not our base case, we don’t rule out US oil export restrictions if the Strait remains effectively closed for longer. Such restrictions may reduce US and global crude and products production, and widen the international vs. US price gap. Many countries have restricted refined product exports, including China, Thailand, and South Korea. The US was a 2.2mb/d net crude importer in 2025 (Exhibit 12), and crude export restrictions would likely depress the WTI price of light US shale oil vs. global benchmarks, raise US crude storage levels, and eventually reduce US shale production. Because many US refineries rely on imported heavier crude, US refinery input costs would decline less than the decline in WTI would suggest and may even rise. The US is a net exporter of refined oil products (Exhibit 12), including gasoline (0.7mb/d) and especially diesel (1.1mb/d). Refined product export restrictions would likely weigh on profits of refiners, and have uncertain effects on US retail fuel prices, that may depend on the product (e.g. diesel vs. gasoline), the region (e.g. US Gulf Coast vs. East Coast), and the scope of restrictions. A restriction of all US oil exports would likely eventually raise US gasoline prices as production cuts by US refineries of all refined products (on lower margins), including gasoline (as US diesel storage hits congestion) outweigh the gain in domestic availability from keeping 0.8mb/d of gasoline in the US. But news on the Iran war over the past few days has raised the question of whether, with energy prices where they are today, the ECB can look through the shock and not hike at all. We would not go that far – at least not yet. With energy prices not far from baseline, surprises would be needed for the ECB to look through the shock. That means either energy prices moving significantly lower, a faster deterioration in economic activity, or gas prices – key for inflation persistence – surprising further to the downside and raising questions about the 2028 inflation forecast. Still, we make two important points. First, while a “look-through” is far from being our baseline, it’s also far from being ruled out. It follows from the discussion above that there is still a non-negligible likelihood of the ECB looking through the shock or potentially waiting a little longer to move. Second, to us, the likelihood of the ECB looking through the shock is higher than that of it hiking more than 50bp. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 9 As argued above, with energy prices not far from baseline, surprises would be needed for the ECB to look through the shock. That said, there is still a non-negligible possibility that the ECB could do that or potentially wait a little longer to move. Non-linear effects on economic activity could be one such surprise. Lower energy prices than in the baseline could be another. And even with energy prices broadly in line with the baseline, they still might not hike – composition matters (Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6). If gas prices continue to surprise on the downside, as they have so far, that could be another rationale for looking through the shock if this led the ECB to question its inflation forecast for 2028. Less of a fiscal response than assumed could do the trick, too. In other words, while a “look-through” is far from being our baseline, it is also far from being ruled out. And at this point, the likelihood of the ECB looking through the shock is higher, to us, than that of it hiking by more than 50bp.

records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 24 April 2026 Citi Research 6 There will be an auction of the new issue JBI31 on May 1. The issue amount is ¥250bn and maturity is March 2036. The coupon is likely to be 0.5%. The Middle East conflict has significantly changed the inflation outlook for FY2026. The YoY growth rate for the core CPI was expected to remain in the 1% range, but it now looks likely to bottom out in April and exceed 2% in the summer. Although it depends on how far government support measures will be expanded, it is reasonable to assume the CPI will remain high for the time being. Normal seasonality will also be a support factor, and we estimate the return from the indexation coefficient through August 10 at 1.7%. The BEI is pricing this good news in and is approaching its previous peak. However, 200bp for the BEI or 50bp for the real yield are key levels to be monitored, and a rise in nominal yields will be necessary to break significantly above these levels. On top of that, even if there is near-term carry real yields are likely to rise more easily than the BEI. Even if long-term inflation achieves 2% on a sustainable basis, JGBIs should trade at low prices due to poor liquidity. Half of the changes in nominal yields since the beginning of the year can be explained by changes in real yields, with the other half by changes in BEI. We think the changes in nominal yields are likely to have a more direct effect on real yields. The current supply/demand environment does not seem bad.

This should reduce the sense of urgency to shore up the labor market among the doves. Indeed, some of the most prominent doves on the committee have changed their tone of late. records.text: An Emphasis on Data Dependence Given the high level of uncertainty, we think that the MPC will want to keep its options open for the upcoming meetings rather than offering a clear signal on the path ahead. That said, Bailey’s recent comments suggest that the Committee will likely adopt a more measured tone than in March and signal a more balanced reaction function to limit the risk of a sharp market reaction of the kind seen after the last meeting. One option would be for the Committee to indicate that it remains ready to act as necessary to keep inflation on track to meet the target, but note that policy decisions will consider the already restrictive policy stance. We also think that the Committee will want to emphasise that policy decisions will be guided by the incoming data on second-round effects rather than depending directly on energy prices, consistent with recent commentary. The risks around our baseline are skewed in a hawkish direction, as the Committee could more explicitly signal a reassessment in June, which would point to greater risks of a near-term hike. Kevin Warsh should support our core positions The market interpreted Warsh’s testimony as lightly bearish, but we found key nuggets of dovishness. For example, he emphasized a preference for a trimmed mean PCE, which is lower than core PCE (Figure 4). We think this is important, as we have argued that the Fed will likely look through the very high inflation prints in certain components, such as computer and software accessories, which are partially why the PCE/CPI wedge is the “wrong way” with PCE over CPI (for a deep dive on this topic, see US Rates Weekly – Rate pause pro tem). Excluding that category—which the trimmed mean does—implies that the bar would be low for rate cuts in late 2026 and throughout 2027. T o be clear, we are not arguing that the Fed will shift targets, but rather that they may look through a few idiosyncratic components that are abnormally high. This is one reason we think there is scope for 1y1y real yields to move lower from here, as it may be trading cheap due to the PCE/CPI wedge. At the same time, Warsh again emphasized the disinflationary nature of AI in the future. The working assumptions seem to be non-linear second-round effects of the oil shock and more fragile inflation expectations and pricing behaviour due to the recent memory of the 2022 inflation shock. Therefore, a prolonged disruption to oil supply constitutes a sufficient condition to warrant a policy response, even without evidence of transmission to other prices. We expect two 25bp hikes in the summer (June and July most probable timing). Any signs of demand weakness and limited passthrough will likely limit stop the hiking in 2H26, but upcoming fiscal spending and private investment will probably make subsequent rate cuts unlikely. We foresee the policy rate staying at 2.50% for the reminder of the forecasting horizon. We see second-round effects into core inflation as far less likely than in 2022. Growth may be more vulnerable than in 2022. records.text: US Economic Presentation23 April 2026 ab 24 Source: BLS, BEA, Federal Reserve, Haver, UBS • The FOMC is in a tough spot. No one wants the losses of a labor market contraction, and everyone wants inflation to get to 2.0%. The funds rate can not do much to stop tariff cost-push inflation, but it can risk making a weak labor market too weak. The same goes for energy prices, a rising downside risk to the labor market expansion. Recall the age- old central banker adage “do no harm.” • Tension in the mandate raises the prospect of more dissents. We expect one 25 bp rate cut in 2026, then two in 2027. The reaction function under a new Chair raises uncertainty and risks around that projection. records.text: Higher Prices and Net Upside Risks For Even Longer While Brent/WTI oil prices have risen this week on still very low Hormuz flows, prices remain below the late March peak, likely because market expectations of Hormuz reopening have reduced the risk premium and led to destocking. Because Hormuz flows remain minimal, we upgrade our Brent/WTI forecasts for 2026Q4 to $90/83 (vs. $80/75 prior) and for 2027 to $85/80 (vs. $80/75 prior) on a later recovery in Hormuz flows and lower Persian Gulf production (Exhibit 1). We now assume a normalization in Gulf exports from mid-May by end-June (vs. our prior assumption of normalization by mid-May) and a slower production recovery, with risks skewed to a more persistent supply shock and higher prices. Exhibit 2 shows why our crude price 2026Q4 forecast is nearly $30 higher than before the Hormuz shock. First, we estimate a $18 net boost to the commercial inventories-based estimate of spot prices vs. long-dated prices (i.e. timespreads) given a 1236mb net hit to global commercial oil inventories by 2026Q4 from the Hormuz shock after the price responses from policy (i.e. release of sanctioned oil on water, release and subsequent replenishing of SPR), lower demand, and higher supply (mostly in the US and Russia). One way to do this would be to change the reference to “additional adjustments” to the policy rate in the forward guidance language to “any adjustments” or simply “adjustments”. This would indicate that the next move wouldn’t necessarily be in the same direction as the previous one. Per the minutes, “some participants judged that there was a strong case for” making such a change in the March statement. These hawks are likely to be just as vocal, and possibly more emboldened by the labor data, at the April meeting. So what next? We see binary scenarios ahead. One where the supply of commodities out of the Middle East starts to normalise in the coming weeks would mean very little chance of policy tightening this year, we think. However, we are near-certain that the Bank would maintain its tightening bias at least until the July meeting (i.e. should the Strait of Hormuz be opened prior to the June meeting, we would not expect a swift BoE pivot). In a scenario where the July forecast can adopt lower commodity futures with a greater degree of certainty is one where cuts start creeping back in as a possibility - although we think from November, at the very earliest, and from February 2027 as a bit more of a likely outcome. In a scenario where disruptions in the supply of oil and gas persist for months, and commodity prices readjust higher, we think hikes become likely - we think 2-3 hikes look probable in this scenario. Should commodity prices move higher in a sustained fashion into the June meeting, we would see a high chance of action then, albeit our modal call would probably be for the hiking cycle to commence from July onwards. There are two serious threats to current prices. The first of course is Energy. The Fed aims to look through direct energy prices, but as these higher fuel prices are passed through to consumers at a much faster rate than in previous cycles, combined with consumers being conditioned to accept higher prices, the potential for pass through to core prices is high. The market clearly overshot, but the concern is that the BoE is becoming less able to influence market pricing. The market is ignoring the Governor’s pushback. Since March, Governor Andrew Bailey has pushed back on hike pricing suggesting the market is getting ahead of itself, most notably in an interview with Reuters, 1Apr26. At the time of that interview the market was pricing 51bp of hikes to December. It is now pricing around 55bp - Figure 5. For sure, the information is changing all the time – most notably the ongoing standoff in the Strait of Hormuz – but the lack of reaction to such direct pushback could be cause for some concern at the BoE. The ability to jaw-bone the market by the Governor is a powerful tool that seems diminished. It could be that the market pays less attention because the Governor can simply be outvoted given the five internal members have very different views. Most notably, the Chief Economist Huw Pill has said that he is “not sure waiting is necessarily the appropriate response” (see Bloomberg, 17Apr26). The Governor is likely to push back, again. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy On tenterhooks The headline see-saw has left EUR rates directionless with the ceasefire extension receiving a tepid response as oil prices remain elevated. Next week, the ECB is likely to signal maximum optionality as it awaits evidence of the conflict's inflationary effect. We recommend paying Sep-26 ECB vs BoE. Excursions and extensions. The Middle East conflict is now into its seventh week and what was characterised as a short excursion is proving to be anything but that. As the second round of talks failed to materialise, President Trump extended the two-week truce announced on April 7 without a firm timeline. Unlike the first iteration of the truce, market reaction to this extension was muted. After all, while it is a relief that missiles are not flying, it is also true that ships are not sailing through Hormuz. Put differently, even as it feels like the right tail of an escalating conflict has likely been attenuated, the headline whiplash and the continued blockade of the Strait are keeping the market on tenterhooks. Figure 1 presents an interesting slice of market shifts since the conflict began. It plots the relative moves in different asset classes versus the % change in Brent, from the time conflict began until the peak (x-axis) and the relative move from the peak until today (y-axis). records.text: Inflation longs still offer hedge value. Inflation fixings continue to price a relatively n short-lived, one-off inflation shock, with no incremental inflation priced beyond May relative to the onset of the conflict (Exhibit 2). As we have observed further out the curve, regressing the changes in sequential inflation implied by the monthly fixings on the corresponding oil future contract suggests that this can at least be partially tied to the lack in risk premium in the oil curve, with a combination of rapid declines in oil demand and anticipation of Hormuz reopening helping to constrain longer-dated futures prices despite still-low flows. This stands in notable contrast to market’s reaction to the energy price shock in 2022, when the whole inflation curve repriced higher—a shift that was subsequently borne out by the longer-lasting inflationary effects of the supply disruptions. While a range of factors differentiate the risks today from 2022, we nonetheless continue to see value in breakeven longs as a hedge to scenarios where oil prices are higher for longer or markets price greater risk of a broadening inflationary impact from supply chain disruptions. We revise the target and stop on our beta-weighted 10y inflation long recommendation to 1.65% and 1.53%, respectively. No sudden shift, but a continued build in large bank UST holdings. records.text: The FX-Rates Relationship in an Energy Shock. Nominal rate differentials have n explained a lower-than-usual portion of daily FX moves throughout the energy shock so far. This is unsurprising given the scale of the vol spillovers from energy and equity markets, but we think other factors are at play as well. First, while rates markets have seen exceptionally large moves throughout the shock, the moves across G10 markets have generally been directionally uniform in response to the ebb and flow in energy prices. This has driven lower realised vol in rate differentials than in outright rates, and it is the former that matters more for FX markets. Second, FX’s relationship to nominal rate differentials specifically has broken down in recent months, while the relationship to real rates has remained more stable. We find that this is typically the case in supply-driven inflation regimes, and we expect this higher relevance of real versus nominal rate differentials to persist so long as ongoing energy shock dominates inflation pricing. While the connection between FX and rates has been disrupted at an aggregate level, narrowing in on intraday correlations meanwhile offers a slightly different perspective. EUR/USD’s beta to nominal rate differentials across 5-minute intervals has flipped to being negative in March and April, isolating for rates-led moves specifically still produces a more ‘typical’ positive beta in April (Exhibit 8). As a reminder, most cash lenders receive a rate close to TGCR while borrowers pay closer to SOFR 75th; therefore, this spread captures dealers’ intermediation costs. Currently at 7bp, the SOFR75/TGCR spread is relatively tight despite the significant increase in T-bills outstanding over the past year. Near term, we expect SOFR will continue fixing at or below IORB as T-bill settlements will continue to be negative for the rest of the month and therefore will not increase collateral funding needs. Into May, we expect Treasury to begin increasing T-bill auction sizes, which would eventually turn Bill settlements positive and over time could push SOFR lightly above IORB. The risk to this view is that Treasury lets the TGA balance run lower through May and June, which would be supportive of repo (i.e., SOFR would likely stay at or under IORB). We expect to learn more about Treasury’s expected funding needs and TGA trajectory at the upcoming refunding announcement on May 6th. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Adding back risk). The ceasefire came at a time when the market had increasingly believed that no off-ramp was in sight, and that boots on the ground were a logical outcome. Instead, the US administration has been actively engaged in investigating off-ramps, and Iran has come to the table, either because of Chinese pressure, or because of wanting to avoid further damages to its infrastructure. A more fundamental argument has been that forward EPS have been rising throughout the period of the conflict for most equity markets, partly driven by semiconductors and/or commodities. We had kept our long US exposure throughout the downdraft, in an overall neutral setting, but on ceasefire day went back to overweight by adding risk in emerging Asia and cutting our Japan underweight. We think the tech outperformance during March was more than just flight to perceived safety and expect tech to remain a leader even after an end to the conflict, which would benefit both the US and emerging Asia. Stay overweight real rates, partly against Gilts. We stay long TIPS. How US rates react to oil spikes depends crucially on how the Fed reacts. Italy (16% of euro area HICP) | Core stable, energy up: We expect Italian HICP to pick up from 1.6%Y in March to 2.6%Y in April, driven largely by energy inflation, which we project to rise by +4.1%M. We forecast another jump in transport fuel prices by 4.5%M as higher oil prices feed through higher inflation. As for electricity and gas, the pass-through from higher oil and gas prices is less clear-cut. For electricity prices, regulated customers are due to see an increase of 8.1%M in their April bills (see here), while we expect a smaller increase in the free market, still positive at around 4.5%. Gas prices should also rise, by around 2.5%M, we think. In contrast, we expect core HICP to remain broadly stable at 1.8%Y. After a sharp fall in March due to the end of the Winter Olympics, we think core will exhibit a similar pattern this year to that of 2025, rising by 1.4%M. Everyone understands that in the context of a supply-side shock, the basic prescription against this is to look through it. I think it's important to understand that the ECB is not against that. If you listen to what Christine Lagarde said in her speech to the ECB watchers conference several weeks ago, she laid out a graduated response function. The first option is for the ECB to look through, but it can look through only if there is a small and transitory inflation shock. But if there is a larger shock to inflation, albeit not too persistent, the ECB is saying that maybe a measured tightening of policy would be more appropriate. At the further end of the spectrum, and again, it's not too much of a surprise, if there is a strong and sustained overshoot of the inflation target, then what the ECB would recommend would be something more forceful and persistent. So really, it's all about gauging the energy shock, how large it's going to be, and how persistent it's going to be. However, costs and benefits are private information for each player, and every round of the war reveals how tough or weak each party is perceived by the other. The longer the war, the tougher Iran is perceived by the US. The more military forces the US deploys in the region, the tougher the US is perceived by Iran. In equilibrium, wars with incomplete information are longer than wars with complete information. Interpreting the war so far In the observed equilibrium so far, the US is implementing a blockade on Iran to make its cost function even more convex, while at the same time proposing a ceasefire to negotiate a deal. Iran is showing no interest. In our framework, it can be interpreted as the US trying to obtain a deal to avoid entering into the very convex segment of its cost function (i.e. avoiding an escalation with boots on the ground). Our forecasts suggest a stronger bullish case for gilts will emerge into 2027 but that is too distant to attach any conviction. Japan The pricing of an April rate hike has receded as uncertainties remain on the Middle East tensions. We think the government will want the BoJ to take only gradual action, and if this is correct, we think standing pat with a hawkish tone would be appropriate. This would mean a stance that suggests a hike in June if the situation stabilizes, and we think the number of votes supporting a rate hike would increase. As the assumed rate hike pace remains steady at 2 hikes per year, we expect a flattening bias between the June and September meeting curve. The 10y JGB yield once tested 2.5% and the 20y JGB yield exceeded the level in January but has since declined. We think rebalancing demand at pension funds will support the market into this month-end. On the other hand, there is a high possibility that fiscal policy discussions such as expanding subsidies for electricity and gas prices will become more active, and the risk premium is likely to be reflected in the 10y sector. If the 5y forward 5y rate rises further under such circumstances, there should be a time when buying will become more active around Japan’s Golden Week holiday. Both OER and PCE housing will be stronger in April, reflecting a catch-up from missed data collections in October. Excluding housing, core services prices should rise 0.31%. We were surprised by a ~1% increase in portfolio management fees in March PPI given declining asset prices starting in February, but still expect a large drag on PCE inflation from financial services prices in April data. Airfares rose moderately in March PPI but remain a bit softer than in CPI. This trend could continue as PCE/PPI airfares have remained stronger over the last ~4 years already. The calculation of legal services prices is a source of uncertainty in March. We expect a modest increase in this component in line with PPI data, but with downside risks if weaker CPI prices are used instead (core PCE could be closer to 0.25%MoM if this is the case). records.text: FX’s beta to real rate differentials has remained more stable Second, we have shown in the past that it is nominal rather than real rate differentials that are typically the clearer driver of FX performance – but there are periods that are important exceptions to that trend, and the current environment is one of them. EUR/USD’s relationship to nominal rate differentials has broken down in recent weeks, with a rolling 3-month beta having fallen sharply to below zero. Energy-driven inflation repricings have played a key role in nominal rate shifts, but the economies with the sharpest inflation repricings are typically also those with the clearest energy vulnerabilities. Those energy vulnerabilities manifest as a currency-negative through a deterioration in its terms of trade, and that pushes in the opposite direction to the usual FX-positive channels of repricings higher in yields. We see this as the clearest explanation for the recent breakdown in FX’s relationship to nominal rates. Real rate differentials meanwhile help to strip out these effects, and have produced a more stable beta for EUR/USD recently (Exhibit 3). The scale of the repricings in traded inflation over the past two months imply strikingly different FX implications from the shifts in nominal versus real rate differentials (Exhibit 4). If the committee delivers a 9-0 vote for an unchanged rate, it might be short-term bullish, as it could imply the committee is not near delivering a hike, so current pricing of tightening in June and July (16bp for each meeting, 32bp in total) would potentially seem too aggressive. But in this scenario, the more lasting point might be that the April meeting sees the MPC setting out its stall out as believer in the transitory nature of the inflationary shock and trusts in its credibility to control medium term inflation — a rerun of Governor King's 2010-11 approach. In the abstract, looking through a supply shock is the "correct" policy response. But that pre-supposes that the central bank's policy credibility alone is enough to anchor inflation expectations. The risk is that the MPC's assessment of its own credibility is at odds with the market's view. In that scenario, the committee runs the risk of being perceived as being "soft" on inflation and that will catalyse a "policy mistake" view that would price the MPC as needing to tighten policy more aggressively in 2027 - ie, a sell-off in 2027's MPC meeting dates as tightening expectation

But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.2% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.3% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 3.8% and to remain 70bp above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. We expect headline inflation falls quickly next year, as oil retraces. But we project price levels at the end of next year to be 30bp above our prior forecast, capturing higher food inflation and some lasting impact on global supply chains. The surge in energy prices is likely to pass through to core inflation as well, with a lag. We now expect 4Q/4Q 2026 core PCE to come in at 3.1%, vs. 2.8% previously. US Economics Weekly 24 April 2026 Citi Research 2 Data released over the week did not substantially change the economic outlook, with jobless claims staying low and retail sales robust. Instead, the primary mover of markets continues to be prospects for a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Interest rates increased along with oil prices this week as effective closure continued and negotiations failed to resume as scheduled. Fed Chair nominee Kevin Warsh delivered testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. Markets took his suggestion that inflation might be “sticky” as hawkish, but we believe he will continue to support rate cuts premised in part on his view that AI will be deflationary. He also mentioned using “trimmed-mean” inflation metrics, which recently have been running lower than other measures of core inflation. While he continued to strongly support a smaller balance sheet, we remain skeptical that Warsh will convince other Fed officials to support a significantly smaller balance sheet. (Read US Economics: Fed-Chair Nominee Warsh emphasizes reform to Fed policy approach for more details) The Justice Department announced on Friday that it is dropping the investigation into the Fed building renovation. This should likely be enough for Senator Tillis to vote in favor of Kevin Warsh as the new Fed Chair. Warsh will likely be confirmed as Chair in time for the June Fed meeting. Powell could still remain on the Board as a Governor as he wants to see the probe final

records.text: Germany In Germany, our tracking estimate has moved down since mid-February, largely reflecting soft retail sales reports and disappointing industrial production data over the first two months of the quarter. Across components, we look for moderation in real consumption growth following the strong +0.7%qoq reading in Q4, as retail sales and hospitality sales both weakened in the first two months of the year. Adverse weather conditions for the construction sector and soft industrial data (including for capital goods ex vehicles) point to a slowdown in real investment growth. Weak goods imports and a rise in both goods and services exports should lead to a positive net trade contribution in Q1, which we expect to be almost entirely offset by a negative inventories contribution. On the GVA side, for all components we expect slower growth in Q1 than in Q4, with industrial and construction production data pointing to outright quarter-to-date declines in the level of activity. On net, we look for a below-consensus +0.1% growth rate (vs. +0.3% in Q4 and consensus at +0.2%). We see risks around this baseline in both directions (Exhibit 5). On the dovish side, Lagarde could argue that energy markets have shown signs of de-escalation, the price data have not been decisive so far and that economic conditions remain very different from 2022, suggesting that the ECB remains in a good position to handle the shock. On the hawkish side, Lagarde could emphasise the inflation risks posed by signs of persistent energy supply disruption, higher energy product prices and potential supply chain disruptions. Moreover, she could flag early signs of higher price and wage setting in the ECB’s surveys. While we believe it is unlikely that she would tee up a June hike in the press conference, she could provide a significant signal by emphasising that the ECB will receive “lots of data” by June to make the appropriate decision. She could also argue that a policy response will likely be required unless energy prices fall back, given that the outlook is tracking in between the baseline and adverse scenario (with the baseline including market pricing for two hikes). records.text: Stuart Jenkins +44(20)7051-4700 | stuart.jenkins@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Global Markets Daily: The FX-Rates Relationship in an Energy Shock 23 April 2026 | 8:01PM BST Nominal rate differentials have explained a lower-than-usual portion of FX price n action over the past two months. This is unsurprising given the recent vol in energy and equity markets, but we think other factors are at play as well. First, while rates markets have seen exceptionally large moves throughout the n shock, the moves across G10 markets have generally been directionally uniform in response to the ebb and flow in energy prices. This has driven lower realised vol in rate differentials than in outright rates, and it is the former that matters more for FX markets. Second, FX’s relationship to nominal rate differentials specifically has broken n down in recent months, while the relationship to real rates has remained more stable. We find that this is typically the case in supply-driven inflation regimes, and we think the ongoing energy shock is a clear example of this. Narrowing in on intraday correlations meanwhile offers a slightly different n perspective. While at a surface level EUR/USD’s beta to nominal rate differentials has flipped to being negative in March and April, isolating for rates-led moves specifically still produces a more ‘typical’ positive beta in April. records.text: The second line of argument, where maybe market participants have a little bit more concern, is that the government may favor a higher inflation regime in Japan because it creates fiscal space. We've written a lot about the fiscal-inflation trade-off in Japan. Very simply, high inflation creates fiscal space. It flatters the nominal GDP denominator, brings debt on a downward path, allows a country to run larger fiscal deficits. For a government that wants to be able to spend more on defense or energy or AI, fiscal space is important. So there's two ways of looking at it. One, genuine economic caution around ensuring the recovery is in a good place. The second, which is a bit more worrying for market participants, is that the government might favor a high-pressure strategy. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 3 With the challenges in Iran continuing, the global economy faces amplified uncertainties. In the short term, a dominant question is how long will the Strait of Hormuz remain closed? Roughly 10 million barrels/day of oil are currently shut in. If sustained, this points to a sizable adverse global supply shock, which could disrupt growth and stoke inflation. In our view, this narrative of “heightened uncertainties” should be balanced against the competing reality of “increased economic resilience. ” As we have underscored in previous work, the global economy has endured a series of adverse shocks in recent years. These have included the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, surging inflation, rapid central bank rate hikes, and President Trump’s evolving tariffs. In each case, the outlook has appeared grim, and we have slashed our forecasts. Global growth, however, has shaken off the shocks and continued at a solid, near- trend pace (Figure 1). The production side of the economy, in particular, is simply more adaptable and flexible than it was a decade or two ago—and thus better able to navigate through even severe challenges. Figure 1. That risk would be amplified if the alternative scenarios are framed in a way that emphasises inflation overshoot, and if the individual paragraphs suggest that only limited additional evidence would be needed before the Committee tightens. In that case, we would expect market pricing to shift towards a higher probability of multiple hikes, beyond the roughly two hikes currently priced, with the trough rate also moving higher. Conversely, dovish risks would stem from a more dovish vote split than in our base case, including a unanimous hold, a more balanced lean in the individual paragraphs, or scenarios and messaging that place greater weight on weaker growth, labour-market downside and the drag from tighter financial conditions. Any scenario framing that downplays inflation persistence and gives greater prominence to the growth trade-off would likely be read as dovish. In that case, we would expect pricing to move back towards a one-hike scenario and to price in a greater degree of curve inversion from 2027 onwards. The government has repeatedly implemented electricity and gas subsidies during peak demand periods in summer and winter. Most recently, large-scale subsidy measures were introduced from January to March 2026. Unlike gasoline subsidies, these are not structured as price caps, meaning that the government sets the scale and duration of the subsidies— and the associated budget—ex ante. While the scale and duration of any new measures remain unclear, a simple benchmark based on the January–March 2026 program—when subsidies totaled ¥ 500bn and amounted to around ¥7,000 per standard model household—suggests that subsidies of (at least) around ¥200bn per month could be implemented during July–September (see New stimulus under the new PM’s expansionary fiscal stance , 21 November 2025). As a result, much of the rise in electricity and gas bills over this summer is also likely to be absorbed by the government rather than by households and corporates ( Exhibit 2). records.text: 14 Europe Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 Compared with the 2022 episode, the Riksbank may be more inclined to respond quickly to persistent upside surprises in energy prices. With fiscal policy clearly expansionary and inflation measures excluding the VAT cut set to rise above target in the coming months, we expect the central bank to hike once back to neutral (2.0%). Economic slack should help contain second‑round effects, limiting the need for a full‑fledged hiking cycle or clearly restrictive policy. We see this more as an end to stimulative rates than the start of any tightening phase. We have limited conviction on the precise timing. We have pencilled in one hike in June, when 1) the persistence of the energy shock should be better reflected in the Riksbank’s forecasts, and 2) the ECB will likely have already delivered its first hike, with second hike likely to follow in July. We doubt that the Riksbank will want to diverge materially from the ECB’s path. That said, a June move remains highly conditional on energy‑market and geopolitical developments in the coming weeks and could easily be delayed. Should geopolitical tensions ease and energy prices normalise faster than we expect, the Riksbank could then remain on hold for longer, adopting a wait‑and‑see stance. GDP expanded 5.0% Y o Y in Q1 2026, a meaningful acceleration from 4.5%Y o Y in 25Q4. Sequential growth held at 1.3%QoQ (NBS seasonal adjusted). The average Total Fertility Rate (TFR) dropped from around 6.0 births per woman in the 1960s to an estimated 1.87 by 2025, well below the replacement level of 2.1. Japan and Korea are aging the fastest, followed by China and Thailand, while India and Indonesia continue to benefit from a longer window of demographic dividends. That said, we believe the demographic drag can be at least partially offset by continued gains in human capital, AI adoption, and more effective retirement‑system management. Even with fewer births, gains in health condition, increased longevity, and technology‑enabled life quality boost would imply a smaller but more capable workforce in the future. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 24 Apr 2026 14:46:16 ET │ 16 pages Canada Economics Weekly Core inflation subdued with soft demand CITI'S TAKE Various data released this week gave some conflicting signals on the near- term inflation backdrop. Headline CPI rose a strong 0.9% MoM in March due to the increase in gas prices, as expected, while core measures were (somewhat surprisingly) still more subdued. Inflation expectations rose in BoC survey data following the jump in energy prices, but very few firms are experiencing difficulty meeting demand. If anything, we would put more weight on the signals of softer core inflation and weak demand, but BoC officials will remain cautious on the risks to inflation expectations. Next week’s April decision may sound more hawkish compared to a dovish March meeting. We still expect further cuts from the BoC this year, but officials may need more evidence in hard data that core inflation is at-or-below target, with the timing of data releases implying cuts may not start up again until September, similar to last year. To expand our analysis, we examine intraday (5-minute) price action throughout the year so far. Consistent with the evolving beta of daily returns, we find that EUR/USD’s beta to nominal rates dropped sharply after the onset of the energy shock at the end of February. But to isolate the FX-rates relationship specifically, we also reduce the intraday sample for each month to windows where oil moves by less than one standard deviation, and where the EU-US 2-year nominal rates differential moves by at least half a standard deviation (with standard deviations estimated within sample in both cases). Narrowing in on 5-minute periods where rate differentials are shifting but oil is relatively stable, we find that EUR/USD’s beta to nominal rates has fallen by less, and has been positive so far in April (Exhibit 6). We see this result as implying that rates-specific shocks can still produce a more ‘typical’ FX reaction in this environment on an intraday basis, and we think this applies to next week’s set of G10 central bank meetings as well. Contemporaneous rules are straightforward - across the board, these would be consistent with near-term hikes, we would assume. The forward-looking Taylor rules are more nuanced. In the upside scenario, we assume these would be signalling at least one hike in the near term (by year-end), with cuts in the second part of the forecast horizon. Likewise, in the downside scenario, forward-looking rules ought to be consistent with cuts by year-end. In the base case, we think the very near term would be consistent with a hold, with mildly higher rates through 2027, and lower through 2028 and 2029. Various inflation and output gap forecasts could be utilised to explain the policy trade- offs. Following the market-implied Bank Rate path in the central scenario means a faster return to target than in the forward-looking Taylor scenario, albeit with a bigger output gap. Following the Bank Rate in the upside scenario means a very slow return to target - vs. the forward-looking Taylor rule-implied path - but also less of a near-term loss in the output gap. records.text: Marija Veitmane 23 April 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Earnings week 2 : still good, but not broadening Another week of 1Q26 earnings confirms a familiar pattern: a small subset of companies is doing well, while the majority are increasingly worried about demand destruction and weakened pricing power. IT and defence remain (somewhat) insulated; stagflation risks dominate the narrative for Consumer and EM CEOs. Market commentary continues to celebrate resilient earnings as a key pillar of the equity rally, even as the Iran war drags on. And to be fair, the US season did start strongly – it had one of the highest proportion of positive surprises since COVID. But the strength — even in the US — is highly concentrated in IT and, increasingly, defence -linked names. We were particularly happy to hear from a few beaten down Software companies that are able to grow their earnings and lock -in future contracts. In contrast, warnings from consumer companies are multiplying. Airline CEOs were particularly grim this week. Consumer Discretionary has delivered the weakest post -earnings performance (Figure 2) and shows the poorest behavioural support, with both institutional investors and hedge funds selling. Emerging markets tell a similarly bifurcated story. Korean and Taiwanese tech companies continue to impress with exceptional growth and margins, while many Chinese stocks are missing already-downgraded expectations. Assuming an average sale price near JPY 60 and a purchase price near JPY 100, lifers may have been net buyers in value terms, but their net buying capacity will likely remain limited in FY26. Robust switching demand pushed average monthly trading volume to JPY 2.09tn, the highest since statistics began in 2004. Looking back at FY25, steady reductions in super-long JGB issuance over the year have eased supply-demand concerns. However, it remains difficult for lifers alone to absorb all super-long supply, and the market will likely continue to rely on demand from foreign and pension investors, whose flows are more uncertain. It is unlikely that the large net buying by foreign investors seen in FY24 and FY25 will continue, and if rate hike expectations recede, there is a risk of significant unwinding of flattener positions. Pension fund demand for domestic bonds also fluctuates with cross-asset performance, so in a scenario of falling equities and a stronger yen, rebalancing could reverse and JGB demand could weaken. Cau- tion regarding super-long supply-demand dynamics remains warranted.
