The 1.5% pace is held back by 1Q residual seasonality in prices, which we put at about 0.4 pct pt (a.r.). After adjusting for that, the underlying pace in 1Q consumption appears to have been about 2% growth—even as tariffs and oil price increases held back real spending. Furthermore, momentum was building throughout the quarter, with real consumption probably rising 0.4% m/m in March. There is more uncertainty around the GDP estimate than normal. Construction spending data and housing starts for February and March have not yet been reported—still delayed by the federal government shutdown. The various construction data will be reported next week before GDP and could affect our forecast. Prices: 1Q core PCE prices rise at a 4.1% q/q annual rate and headline PCE at 4.3%. Private domestic final purchases (consumption plus investment) rises at a 2.2% q/q annual rate, 0.2 pct pt below its average over the past year. Consumption slows slightly, but nonresidential fixed investment rises at a strong 6.6% pace—depending in part on what the business construction spending data for February show. records.text: 16 Europe Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 We think a move at one of the next meetings is almost a done deal, and our base case is a hike at the June meeting. After that, we would expect Norges Bank to retain a hawkish bias, keeping the door clearly open to an additional hike in 2H26 should the data warrant it. That said, our growth and core inflation projections for 2H26 are below Norges Bank’s new forecasts, which makes us sceptical that the Bank will ultimately deliver a second hike that would take rates back to the 2024 peaks – though we think it remains a close call. Looking ahead to next year, we see scope for two cuts (March/June), bringing the policy rate back to 3.75%. Could Norges Bank move as early as May? Yes – we think the meeting will be live. With uncertainty high and rate expectations volatile, waiting until June while maintaining a hawkish stance makes sense to us. The March core inflation print was broadly in line with the Bank’s projections, and there is limited data due before the meeting. That said, some Committee members already considered a hike in March, so the decision could be finely balanced. In the event of a May hike, we think another near‑term move (e.g., a hike in June/July) would become a more material risk, followed by a hold through the rest of the year and cuts in 1H27. The drop in crude oil imports is yet to come Real imports fell 5.5% m/m in March, but this largely reflected payback from February’s 6.8% increase and came as no surprise (+1.0%q/q in Q1). The last large crude oil tanker passing through the Strait of Hormuz arrived in Japan on 3 April, meaning that March crude oil import volumes still increased by 2.4%y/y on a quantity basis, with no visible impact from the Middle East conflict yet. Imports via the Strait of Hormuz account for 93% of total crude oil imports, making a decline from April onward unavoidable. At the same time, the government has been advancing substitute procurement from routes outside the Strait of Hormuz. In April, it is expected to secure about 20% of last year’s actual import volume, rising to around 60% in May. Most of this substitute procurement will come from the Middle East via routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. In addition, imports from the US are expected to quadruple—from 90,000 barrels per day to 360,000 barrels per day. In other words, the remaining 40% will need to be covered by strategic petroleum reserves. As of 20 April, Japan’s crude oil reserves stood at the equivalent of 215 days (about seven months). records.text: 7 23 April 2026 inventory drawdowns have provided temporary relief, keeping refiners operational and preventing an immediate price spike. However, the pressure is visible in physical markets, with near-term paper prices running $20–$40 above the forward curve, a spread that is typically only $1–$2. Based on current drawdown trajectories, global inventory levels including strategic reserves are expected to reach critical thresholds by the second week of May. Should market participants begin to price in an extended disruption, oil prices could rise significantly, potentially reaching $150–$200 per barrel. At that point, physical supply constraints and forced demand destruction would become the central dynamic. While this tail risk is not embedded in the base case, it remains a critical factor to monitor. IMF World Economic Outlook: The uneven impact of the war The global economy entered 2026 on a strong footing but now faces a major resilience test from the war; the duration and scope of the conflict are key. Global growth was much more resilient than expected in 2025 on the back of trade de- escalation, easy monetary conditions, fiscal support and the AI boom. Pre-conflict, global growth was expected to remain at a healthy 3.4% in 2026, similar to the 2025 outturn. Heightened uncertainty has prompted the IMF to enumerate three scenarios for 2026. However, GoodLeap’s structure differs materially from typical short-term deferrals: it offers extended deferral periods of 3-18 months, after which accrued interest is capitalized and the loan re-amortizes over a 10-year term based on actual prepayments received. nSame-As-Cash (SAC) Non-Deferred loans. SAC Non-Deferred loans is similar to the standard P&I loans in requiring immediate payments, but with a critical distinction: during the promotional period (up to 24 months), monthly payments apply entirely to principal while interest accrues but remains uncollected. records.text: Global Asset Allocation 24 April 2026 Citi Research 7 Europe: sentiment still bearish, remain neutral. While the news flow on the US- Iran war has been broadly positive since the end of March escalation, sentiment in Europe is starting to resemble more the sharp drop in 2022 because of the Russia- Ukraine war (Figure 10). The latest ZEW expectations for the month of April came in at -17.2, against more benign economists’ expectations of -5.8. From an energy perspective, Europe today sits in a much better place relative to 2022. Also thanks to contained NatGas prices relative to the 2022 war, it is hard to get excited about local equities. Broad equity markets have bounced back after the ceasefire avoided worst-case outcomes (i.e. energy infrastructure destruction), retracing much of the war-led selloffs. But markets more closely dependent on oil (either because of the manufacturing exposure, the oil import exposure, or both), have yet to retrace the sell off fully, like Europe. Our simple signal to be long European equities, as mentioned before, is based on IFO and/or ZEW expectations being above their 3m moving average, and it’s far from triggering. The commodities terms of trade shock weighs more on Europe than other markets, and with a heavy cyclical exposure, we would consider a long only after a full resolution is in sight and oil retraces its gains. records.text: April FOMC Preview: On Hold Ahead of the Leadership Transition The FOMC is likely to reiterate its wait-and-see message at its April meeting this week because the war with Iran continues to cloud the economic outlook and to present risks to both inflation and activity. Our April Fed Chatterbox noted that most participants see the current policy stance as leaving the FOMC in a good place to remain on hold while it evaluates news about the war and its impact on the economy. We expect a strong consensus to stay on hold, with only one dissent from Governor Miran, as in March. The FOMC’s post-meeting statement is likely to leave the policy guidance unchanged. While the minutes to the March meeting noted that “some” participants saw “a strong case for a two-sided description of the Committee’s future interest rate decisions,” recent comments from participants indicated that most still expect the next move to be a cut, and there is little additional reason to make a change now that the FOMC chose not to in March. We expect small changes to the statement to note the better labor market news and higher inflation numbers. The FOMC could drop “job gains have remained low” and leave only “the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months,” or it could note that job gains have picked up and have been roughly in line with slower labor force growth on average. records.text: European Rates Weekly 23 April 2026 Citi Research 10 Belgium faces increasing rating pressure owing to increasing government deficit, weak growth perspectives and high debt levels. Moody’s already downgraded it to single-A category, and we see elevated risks that S&P will follow suit. Whilst Belgium trades wider than Spain and Italy, its richness versus OATs is increasingly hard to justify on a fundamental basis. However, given its lower funding needs and more front-loaded issuance profile, BGBs are likely to stay in a tight range versus OATs. Similarly, the EU has outperformed BGBs since June last year, suggesting that Belgium’s weakening fundamentals are already largely in the price. Belgian sovereign ratings are under pressure. Moody’s downgraded Belgium to A1 (Stable) from Aa3 (Negative) on 17 April citing concerns around its fiscal outlook, growth perspectives and increasing debt-to-GDP levels owing to fiscal deficits remaining elevated. Following the downgrade, Moody’s rating is now on par with Fitch, with both in the single-A category, whereas S&P still rates Belgium two notches higher at AA. This makes Belgium the fourth EMU-11 country (along with Spain, Portugal and Ireland) where there is a two-notch difference between the major rating agencies assessments (Figure 14). Figure 14. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 14 Canada GDP growth contracted in Q4 2025 but with a stronger increase in domestic demand. Consumption is likely to grow in Q1 but headwinds such as slower population growth, weakening labor market and higher gasoline prices should weigh on consumers this year. The spike in energy prices could provide some boost to growth through larger exports of oil but on net we still expect slow growth this year. Employment growth was modest in March after a couple months of declines. In general, employment growth has been volatile but likely around a broadly declining trend. The unemployment rate has stayed within a range around 6.5- 7%. Wage growth was very strong in March but likely impacted by some compositional and base effects issues. We expect the unemployment rate to remain elevated in 2026 as labor demand continues to weaken despite slower population growth putting downward pressure on the unemployment rate. The 3-month annualized run rate of the core inflation measures has slowed to below 2%. Higher energy prices boosted headline inflation in March to 2.4%YoY but core measures remained soft. Data like a jump in CFIB price plans keeps us cautious on some near-term risks of stickier core inflation in Q2, similar to last year. But also like last year, we expect softer demand to ultimately keep core inflation subdued and for the BoC to be cutting rates again later in the year. Home prices and forward-looking indicators

records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 24 April 2026 Citi Research 2 Data released this week paint a conflicting picture for inflationary pressures. Headline CPI jumped as expected while core measures remained surprisingly subdued. Inflation expectations were higher in BoC survey data, but difficulty meeting demand remains very low. Overall, we would put more weight on the signals of softer core inflation and weak demand, keeping us expecting rate cuts by the BoC later this year. But officials will likely be a bit more cautious on the upside risks to inflation expectations and could sound more hawkish in their April decision next week compared to a dovish March meeting. Somewhat stronger growth data since March also keep officials a bit more comfortable leaving policy rates on hold while incoming data reveal more about the inflation risks. As such, with a data release calendar that only includes two more CPI reports before the July BoC meeting, September now seems like the more likely time for a restart of rate cuts. This would give BoC officials time to see inflation data up through July CPI. Like a number of other developments this year, this timeline would also echo last year and align with our base case for further rate cuts from the Fed premised on weaker US labor market data over the summer. A clear positive turn in this week’s UK data stands in contrast to a deterioration in the Euro area, reversing part of the underperformance in UK data that was a key theme of last year (Exhibit 2). There are caveats and quality concerns around many of these UK releases, but at an aggregate level we think resilient data has been a key source of recent support for the currency. Other domestic considerations meanwhile present more of a challenge to Sterling in our view. Our economists think the BoE is unlikely to meet the material hike premium priced by markets for this year, the currency is still highly overvalued on our structural GSDEER metric, and bouts of fiscal and political risk premium remain a risk. The latter continues to be a market focus ahead of the May 7 local elections, and while we would stress that Sterling’s imprint from political uncertainty over prior months has been much more tactical than fundamental, we still see the risks to the currency as asymmetrically negative from this angle. All told, while Sterling should remain highly levered to any further recovery in global risk sentiment, its energy-importer attributes and the balance of the UK’s domestic macro themes still imply more value in the negative side of its distribution. records.text: hiring, worries of a self -fueling labor downturn have been prevalent in both market and Fed discussions. The job market, at worst, has been normalizing. Quantified from both an unemployment rate and unemployment claims perspective, Labor markets are still at histo rically strong levels. When measured from a job creation level, yes, job growth had been slowing, but this is not necessarily a sign of labor weakness. Labor supply is bumping up against record levels as labor force participation nears some of its highest levels on record for the prime aged population (25 - 54) without a spike in the UER. Figure 13Labor market remains quite strong Source: State Street Markets, US BLS This combination of participation and UER puts the current labor market in continued top tier territory historically. The Fed’s dual mandate gives them options on whether to prioritize jobs or prices, yet jobs is inherently a much more sociopolitical item than prices are. In fact, the creation of the dual mandate which replaced the inflation mandate was seen as more politically driven than it was economically. What is the effective level of NAIRU? Not an easy question to answer ex-ante. We can model ourselves to death, but real-world evidence show that as inflation remains above target and disinflationary trends have long since ended prior to the recent conflict, at the very worst, the UER is at a neutral rate. The Fed has chosen to prioritize a strong labor market over squashing inflationary forces .

This environment is also fostering "capital recycling, " where major CMBS sponsors may opportunistically dispose of midscale assets, creating a pipeline of opportunities for buyers focused on the midscale segment. The foundation of the midscale segment's stability rests on its ability to manage its single largest operating expense: labor. With labor costs climbing from approximately 49% of total revenue in 2023 to nearly 56% by the end of 2026, and with wage inflation projected to add another 3% to 4% in 2026, midscale operators are aggressively adopting AI and automation to protect margins (Figure 5 & Figure 6). This strategic pivot is not merely an enhancement but a core defense against expense volatility. By implementing AI-driven tools, operators are directly targeting this massive cost center. With fiscal policy clearly expansionary and inflation measures excluding the VAT cut set to rise above target in the coming months, we expect the central bank to hike once back to neutral (2.0%). Economic slack should help contain second‑round effects, limiting the need for a full‑fledged hiking cycle or clearly restrictive policy. We see this more as an end to stimulative rates than the start of any tightening phase. We have limited conviction on the precise timing. records.text: M Idea 10 On positioning, as has occurred many times in the past few years, disappointment about easing has prompted unwinds of crowded money market longs in delta one and option format, exacerbating the sell-off. Client views have remained firmly tilted to bullish duration, with reasoning similar to ours. Trading-wise, implementation has been both delta one and via options, but overall positioning is materially lighter than pre-conflict. We discussed the reasoning behind our long duration recommendation in Open Longs in Intermediates. To repeat: 1) The long end - especially in real terms - has not caught up with the retracement seen elsewhere. 2) Cross-market long-dated euro rates have underperformed the most since the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East. 3) We do not see the underperformance as justified by expectations of higher fiscal spending in the region. 4) Looking at the behavior of German swap spreads and intra-EMU spreads there is little indication of strong concerns about fiscal expansion in other parts of the fixed income landscape. 5) Last week has seen a resumption of syndicated issuance after a hiatus, but we do not see excessive supply pressures in the short term given that a great number of deals were executed before the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East. • Trade idea: Maintain long 5y2y €str, entered at 2.93%, with a target at 2.70% and a stop at 3.10%.

The IMF’s April 2026 World Economic Outlook showed a modest downward revision of 0.3%-pt to growth in its reference forecast. Under the reference baseline scenario, the conflict ends soon with disruptions not extending beyond the first half of this year and progressively normalizing in the second half of 2026. The IMF report indicated that the global growth outlook was tracking toward an upward revision of 0.1% before the war but ultimately revised down by 0.3%-pts due to higher oil prices. This view is based on a relatively benign outcome for the Middle East conflict and is called a “reference” forecast rather than a “baseline”. Under this scenario, energy prices rise about 19%, global growth slows to 3.1% from 3.4% and inflation accelerates to 4.4% in 2026. The revision to the IMF growth outlook is about one-half the 0.6%-pt revision implied by our global modeling of the oil shock, but in line with the bottom-up J.P. Morgan forecast revision since the start of the war of about 0.2%-pt. However, our assumption is that oil averages about $90/bbl this year (peaking this quarter at $100), while the IMF assumes an average price this year of just a touch over $80/bbl. Our oil forecast is thus a bit closer to the IMF’s adverse scenario of an average price of $100/bbl this year, for which their outlook slashes growth by 1.3%-pt. records.text: M Idea 2 AI is adding to productivity growth To better understand AI and the US economic transition, our recent publications examined prior innovation waves: AI, like prior general purpose technologies, can be expected to increase productivity and create temporary labor displacement, among other effects. Another report found that AI adoption is causing minimal labor market disruptions, so far —small upward pressure on the unemployment rate (of about 0.1 pct pt). In another report, we asked whether AI is leading to faster productivity growth, and we summarize that report here. We found evidence that since the start of 2025, industries with greater AI exposure have been leading faster productivity growth (Exhibit 1 ). To estimate labor productivity, we constructed industry-level measures of output per employee using the BEA's industry output data and BLS payrolls. We assigned each industry a measure of AI exposure using the criterion in Felten et. al. (2021). From there, we grouped various industries into three categories: top-25% AI exposure, middle-50% AI exposure, and lowest-25% AI exposure. We find positive correlation between industry-level AI exposure and growth in output per employee. We estimate that industries with high AI exposure contributed 1.7pp of the 2.4pp growth in productivity in the four quarters through 4Q 2025. The Committee’s post-meeting statement is likely to acknowledge the better labor market news and higher inflation numbers but to leave the standing policy guidance unchanged. We expect a strong consensus to stay on hold for now, with only one dissent, as in March. The announcement that the Department of Justice is dropping its investigation n of Chair Powell has cleared the way for Kevin Warsh to be confirmed as the new chair. records.text: e global economy in recent years has endured the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, surging inflation, rapid central bank rate hikes, and President Trump’s evolving tariffs. In each case, the economy has successfully shaken off the shocks, and growth has continued at a solid, near-trend pace. Longer-Term Lessons from This Episode—Countries are likely to diversify their energy sourcing to avoid concentrated dependence on any single supplier or geographical chokepoint. For example, flows through the Strait have accounted for 60% of Korea’s oil consumption and nearly 50% of Japan’s. Countries are also likely to take steps toward increased energy independence. This could include tapping undeveloped energy resources, boosting strategic oil inventories, and increasing reliance on nuclear power and renewables. Reforming the International Economic System—The evolving policies of the Trump Administration have led to intensified introspection by policymakers around the world regarding the features and functioning of the global economic order. We are clearly in a period of flux—in our view comparable to the unwinding of the Bretton Woods system in the early 1970s—and the situation requires fresh thinking and perspectives. Such reforms can be complex and difficult. But they also have the potential to bring important new opportunities. The fundamental argument of the Trump Administration is that the economic order that has prevailed in recent decades requires the US to give too much, while it receives too little. As evidence the Administration points to declining US manufacturing employment, sustained US trade deficits, and the heavy defense spending by the United States compared with many of its allies (Figures 13 & 14). In other words, the cost of US global leadership has simply been too high. The Trump Administration sees itself as working to level the playing field. While each of these points is analytically debatable, this narrative captures the general perspective of many US voters. For example, these general points are echoed by many left-wing voices as well. Previous generations of US voters would have broadly agreed that US global leadership—and US efforts to make the world safer, more prosperous, and more equitable—would ultimately redound to the benefit of the United States. But that consensus now appears to have frayed. The IMF highlights that the growth of NBFIs, including hedge funds and leveraged ETFs, are amplifying equity and bond market volatility, threatening to exacerbate market stress in the event of a market downturn. In particular, non-resident NBFI investment poses risks for emerging markets, where capital flows are highly volatile and sensitive to shifts in global risk sentiment. The IMF GFSR calls for enhanced supervision of NBFIs, stricter data collection, and increased readiness of central bank liquidity facilities to handle potential disruption in these markets. There is a need to close information gaps in non- bank finance and strengthen oversight of derivative-related exposures as these institutions have become major players in cross-border portfolio flows. The conflict has led to a significant rise in energy prices, but we think it’s too soon for the BoE to have enough evidence to be convinced to act in response to the energy shock. Data so far has been somewhat hawkish but show limited decisive evidence on the fallout from the conflict. Moreover, comments from BoE Governor Bailey noting that he is in no rush to raise rates imply that the bar for an April hike is fairly high. At the same time, energy prices lower than the highs is also likely to reduce urgency. We expect the ECB to keep rates on hold, while retaining full optionality to hike at a later point should the data warrant this. Absent a significant and sustained fall in energy prices (not our central case), we ultimately expect the data to support a 25bp rise at the June meeting. In the UK, a string of stronger-than-expected releases has added fuel to the fire for the BoE to deliver a hike, evidenced by last week’s steep repricing of front-end rates. We ultimately expect the policy committee to err on the side of caution, voting 7-2 to stay on hold, with two members casting the first votes for a rise. However, we anticipate a distinctly hawkish tone – demonstrated through higher inflation projections, broadly unchanged guidance and the dissent in favour of hiking – that leaves the door open to tighten in the future. We continue to expect two 25bp rate hikes this year, starting in June. The BoJ also has an important decision this week. Considering the ongoing uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict and the apparent lack of government support, we expect the policy rate to remain unchanged. Spain (12% of euro area HICP) | Energy driving headline lower: For Spain, we expect both headline CPI and HICP inflation to step down by around 40bp to 3.0%Y. The main driver is energy, particularly electricity. Our tracking already points to softer electricity prices this month, but, more importantly, the bulk of the effect from the fiscal measures implemented on 22 March should be felt in April. In the case of electricity, we estimate that around ⅔ of the 11pp VAT cut will feed through to final prices, affecting both the regulated and free markets. A similar dynamic applies to gas, where VAT cuts should also translate into lower prices, although the impact on headline inflation is more muted given gas’s significantly lower weight relative to electricity. For fuels and lubricants, our tracking suggests petrol prices at the pump are down by around 8%M. This decline is likely to be partially offset by an increase in diesel prices, leaving an overall reduction in fuels and lubricants of roughly 1%M for the month. Turning to core inflation, we expect HICP core to fall by around 30bp, while CPI core declines by a more modest 15bp. A sufficient rise in EUR can put downward pressure on inflation and growth and risk undermining the ECB's 2% inflation target. Given that higher energy prices increase imported inflation, has the ECB's tolerance of a higher EUR increased? Theoretically, we think this argument has merit, but investors will likely seek clearer confirmation, particularly around the specific levels that may, or may not, trigger discomfort or a dovish monetary policy response. In discussions with investors, we sense that, if anything, conviction around a weaker USD thesis and a higher EUR/USD has risen. Investors are increasingly considering not just 1.20, but also 1.30, suggesting the ECB's limits on patience may increasingly come into focus.

The ‘Reflation trade (or Takaichi trade)’ regime for Japan markets really kicked off last year July, when following a bruising defeat of the LDP in the upper house elections, the odds of Sanae Takaichi as new PM started rising. The policy mix offered by the new candidate was perceived as expansive on fiscal and looser on monetary policy, meaning higher local equities, lower JPY, and steeper curve. We expect to see the BoE as using the Riksbank as a template. Their March MPR mixed higher commodity prices and second round effects in the upside scenario that they judged as warranting near-term hikes. Their downside scenario, meanwhile, featured the same market-based commodity prices as their base case, but assumed a bigger hit to growth and lesser second-round effects; in this scenario, near-term cuts were warranted. records.text: ink the muted moves in MYR rates thus far may be explained from two perspectives. Firstly, markets have been more inclined to pay front-end rates in countries that are large net oil importers and highly exposed to the Middle East, and Malaysia ranks relatively low on this front. Secondly, Malaysia has maintained fixed petrol prices at RM1.99/litre throughout the conflict, whereas most other countries in the region have started to allow some pass-through of fuel prices (Figure 3). However, we have some reservations about these arguments. Firstly, despite being an oil exporter, Malaysia remains a net energy importer and exposed to the Middle East, with a quarter of its imports coming from that region (see FX: Asia's sensitivity to supply-driven energy shocks, dated 10 March). Secondly, with energy prices expected to remain structurally elevated over the medium term, second-round effects will start to filter through to Malaysia via neighboring economies, putting upward pressure on inflation over time. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 We think Powell’s core message will be that the Fed is firmly on hold and policy is “well positioned” to respond to risks to both mandates. Powell will probably get asked about the forward guidance language, whether or not it changes, and the threshold for hikes. If he repeats that hikes are not the base case for the majority of the committee, markets will read that as dovish. If he sounds more open minded to hikes (e.g., if he emphasizes the importance of finishing the job on inflation or the fact that inflation has overshot the target for five years), that would be hawkish. We wouldn’t expect him to provide quantitative thresholds for rate hikes. Regarding the war, we think Powell will note both the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to the labor market and growth. But which way will he lean? If his comments mirror those of Daly (mentioned above), markets would read that as very hawkish. Powell could get asked about the pickup in the labor data. We think he’ll probably caution against over-reacting to a few data points, and state that the broad labor data have been soft but stable (Exhibit 2). A dovish response would note that wage inflation has been weakening. A more hawkish answer would lean into downside risks to the u-rate, even if they are mostly due to slowing labor supply. Core inflation down on a large drop in services inflation on Easter base effects: We forecast core inflation to fall to 2.1%Y from 2.3%Y as services inflation declines to 3.0%Y from 3.2%Y (almost 30bp unrounded). The main reason for the large step down in services inflation is base effects from volatile tourism-related items. In 2025, Easter was relatively late in April, which raised airfare prices that month in particular, and the earlier date this year (5 April) implies less price pressures, all else equal. Higher jet fuel prices may bring a small offset. Aside from volatile items, we note continued softening in measures of underlying services inflation since the start of the year. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 Next Week: Fed, ECB, BoE, Euro area inflation, and 1Q26 GDP Euro area | ECB, April inflation, and 1Q26 GDP: Next week will be a busy one in the euro area. The data focus will be on the flash April inflation print publishing on Thursday. For the euro area, we forecast headline at 2.9%Y (up from 2.6%Y) and core at 2.1%Y (down from 2.3%Y). Higher energy inflation drives the headline upside and lower services inflation on Easter base effects weighs on core (details in our Inflation Preview here). We get first country prints on Wednesday, for Spain (MSe 3.0%Y) and Germany (MSe 3.0%Y), with France (2.2%Y) and Italy (2.6%Y) out on Thursday. We also receive the first estimate for GDP in 1Q26 GDP on Thursday, where we look for signs of the energy shock and expect only a modest increase at the euro area level at 0.1%Q. German retail sales publishing for March is one of the first hard data points to potentially show an impact on consumption (MSe -2.0%M). We will also keep an eye on the ECB Bank Lending Survey to check whether demand for credit softened and/or credit conditions tightened since January. On policy, the key focus will be on the ECB Governing Council meeting. We expect the ECB to remain on hold and think that the Council will want to keep all options on the table, which will prevent any firm signalling in either direction, hike or hold in June (detail in our ECB Preview here). Inflation risks have shifted back to the fore as fuel prices reassert themselves, effectively closing the door to further monetary easing and anchoring policy in a prolonged hold. The central issue, however, is fiscal-political execution. President Kast’s reform agenda is ambitious but met early with legislative fragmentation, complicating fiscal signaling and delaying confidence gains. While medium-term fundamentals remain sound, near-term outcomes will depend less on macro mechanics and more on whether governance frictions ease quickly enough to unlock investment. Colombia Macro backdrop weakened further as inflation persistence drove aggressive monetary tightening amid rising institutional tensions. Services-led inflation and embedded wage effects are keeping expectations elevated, limiting policy flexibility despite slowing activity. Fiscal credibility remains a concern, as some financing approaches could obscure underlying structural spending pressures. Political factors increasingly appear to be influencing the economic outlook, as rising tensions between the executive and key institutions and an increasingly polarized election cycle have turned governance risk into a macro variable. Markets appear to be looking past the remainder of the current administration, with the June runoff increasingly being seen as an inflection point for policy consistency and medium-term stabilization. records.text: scorecard summarises trading signals for US, German, and UK rates (10Y yields and 2s/10s curves). Scorecard values range from -5 to +5 and are calibrated on each signal’s historical distribution. Scorecard values are not directly comparable across markets or indicators, as each reflects the relative position of its own signal within its historical context and does not indicate the absolute strength or intensity of the view. Individual signals are mapped to the -5/+5 scorecard scale based on their percentile rank within their historical distribution using a starndard lookback period as in our GFIMs publications for fair value models and a 2Y lookback period for the other variables. For the momentum model, we simply rescale the -20/+20 model signal to the -5/+5 scorecard scale dividing by 4. JPM policy rate call bias reflects the J.P. Morgan Hawk-Dove Bias Index and indicates whether J.P. Morgan’s 1Y-ahead policy rate forecasts are more hawkish or dovish than market pricing. Fair value models show the residuals from regressing 10Y and 2s/10s curves against drivers (front-end OIS rates, central bank balance sheets, vol etc.) over the past 1Y history. Positioning indicators aggregate information from J.P. Morgan’s Client surveys and our Active Bond fund positioning models (see here for US and here for Euro); long investor positioning from these indicators corresponds to short signal in the scorecard. What markets are mispricing As we discussed last week, markets are assuming the end of the war depends on the US as it was the case with trade wars last year. Therefore, it is optimal for markets to expect a short and contained war. But what is not priced in is a scenario where Iran manages to keep the Strait closed for longer to maximize its deterrence effect. In this case, a correction in the stock market would make the US cost curve more convex. The equilibrium of this war can be longer than what the market is pricing, because the all involved parties, including the market and other passive players, have not experienced enough pain to capitulate. As a result, this could have economic consequences that are not currently priced in. The inevitable inefficiency of wars Therefore, with private information, wars are longer and more inefficient because the marginal costs already paid become sunk costs and the only relevant economic calculation is the expected benefit of continuing the war relative to the expected cost. records.text: M Idea 8 Rates Strategy: A Nuanced Set-up for the Front-End Fabio Bassanin We have limited conviction on the market reaction to the April MPC, as the price action will depend not only on the headline decision, but also on the framing of the scenarios, the signal from the policy rules, the eventual vote split and the tone of the individual paragraphs. Our base case remains a hawkish hold, with an 8:1 split and Pill voting for a hike. On the messaging, we expect a somewhat more balanced tone than in March, with the opening paragraphs of the minutes likely to emphasise the high degree of uncertainty around the outlook. That said, the BoE could still retain a tightening bias, linked to a judgement that the risks of second-round effects are rising, rather than to evidence that such effects have already emerged. The market reaction will therefore depend on which element dominates. If markets focus primarily on the inflation risks, front-end rates could remain priced for a significant degree of further tightening. If greater weight is placed on the growth trade-off, the response could prove more supportive for duration. More broadly, the framing of the scenarios, the vote split and the lean in the individual paragraphs could tilt the market reaction in either direction. That said, the hawkish market reaction to the March MPC may itself argue for a more carefully balanced tone this time around. records.text: helter (January 12, 2026), Barclays economists laid out an elegant analytical structure to model CPI rents with the Zillow Observed rent Index (ZORI) using an error correction model framework. At the time, they identified three scenarios to help think through risks to rent of primary residence and owners' equivalent rent: • A base case scenario, in which the ZORI index is sustained at 0.15% m/m from December• onward; • a downside scenario, where ZORI grows 0.05% m/m (about 0.6% saar); and• • an upside scenario, where ZORI grows 0.25% m/m (about 3.0% saar).• With that context in mind, the last six realized ZORI prints have been: 17bp, 10bp, 9bp, 4bp, 7bp, and 6bp - relatively close to the downside scenario ( Figure 2). In January, our economists noted that the downside scenario was consistent with a run rate of 14bp (1.69% annualized) for OER and 13bp (1.57% annualized) for rent of primary residence by the end of 2027. Moreover, the single-family ZORI has taken a leg lower to ~15bp m/m (from 25bp m/m for much of 2025) while multi-family ZORI has decelerated from a run rate of ~15bp m/m to near 0bp (in fact, slightly negative in March 2026). 23 April 2026 17 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Holding pattern

records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 22 India El Nino risks emerge, IMD predicts weak monsoon: Weather events could intensify supply side shocks as El Nino risks emerge and IMD’s first monsoon forecast puts rainfall at 8% below long period average (LPA). T o put this forecast in context, we looked at IMD’s first monsoon forecast in 8 Global El Nino years that we have had this century. Only once in those 8 years did the IMD start its monsoon forecast with a “below normal” prediction and this 8% below LPA forecast is the lowest in this century. Historically, El Niño years often lead to droughts, reduced agricultural production and Agri GVA, and increased food grain inflation as seen during the 2023 El Niño episode. Benign core inflation faces weather and energy shocks: March's headline inflation reached a 14-month high of 3.4%YY. Cooking gas price saw an increase, but the broader energy category and underlying core CPI (excluding precious metals at 2.1%YY) showed muted pressure, indicating limited impact from geopolitical conflicts. But inflation momentum could rise due to: (1) some uptick in petrol/diesel prices, (2) food supply risk from below normal monsoon (IMD forecast 8% below LPA) and (3) impact of other supply-chain disruptions (higher shipping costs and fertilizer prices). Beyond demand and supply, we suspect the post-Brexit era has seen potential structural shifts in the product markets (food and manufacturing) where more pricing power might be concentrated with suppliers remaining in a smaller market outside the large EU customs union. records.text: Japan Economics 24 April 2026 Citi Research 2 March nationwide CPI: Core inflation looks set to rise towards 2% again The nationwide core CPI (excluding only fresh food) increased 1.8% YoY in March, up from a 1.6% climb in February and overshooting the market projection (+1.6%) (see Figure 1). Meanwhile, CPI excluding fresh food and energy, i.e., core-core CPI, rose 2.4% YoY in March, down modestly from 2.5% YoY in February and matching the market projection. The version of core CPI using US definitions, i.e., CPI excluding food other than alcoholic liquor and energy, increased 1.4% YoY in March, as in February. The main driver for higher inflation has been rising energy prices following the escalation in the Middle East conflict. With gasoline prices declining less YoY (- 5.4% YoY in March vs. -14.9% YoY in February), energy’s contribution to core CPI inflation increased from -0.75ppt in February to -0.47ppt in March. Meanwhile, food inflation continued to slow, resulting in a 0.12ppt drop in the contribution of food other than fresh food. In the past few months, core CPI has slowed to below 2%, reflecting subsidies for electricity and gas bills as well as the abolition of provisional tax surcharges for gasoline. She stated that the DOJ has requested the Fed’s Office of Inspector General to scrutinize the cost overruns and that she expects a report on the findings soon. However, she also stated that she will “not hesitate to restart a criminal investigation should the facts warrant doing so.” This news represents an about-face relative to just a few days ago ( 18 minutes , 4/22/2026). US rates are still lacking the potential catalysts to durably lower yields that would come from either de-escalatory relief or growth downside concerns. But the higher starting level of yields and rates’ diminished sensitivity to oil moves continue to favor positive carry expressions for now, with inflation longs still a useful hedge against more protracted and/or disruptive outcomes. The gradual rise in energy prices and inflation risk were a headwind to carry trades in Europe ahead of the ECB and BoE meetings. We favor long sovereign credit and long inflation in Europe, while we prefer front-end longs in Gilts after a period of 10y outperformance on the curve. While recent data point to significant indirect effects as companies pass through increased fuel costs, we do not think this will dissuade the Committee from a “wait-and-see” strategy at this meeting given limited evidence so far of second-round effects via wages. An 7-2 vote looks most likely, with Chief Economist Pill and external member Greene preferring a 25bp hike. We think the updated MPC projections will show headline inflation rising notably n to around 3.4% in 2026H2 given higher energy prices, but dropping below target to 1.7% by the end of the forecast horizon because of a higher conditioning path for Bank Rate. We expect the growth projection to be lowered by around 0.8pp cumulatively over the forecast horizon. The policy projections are likely to show a mixed picture, with the optimal policy path pointing to near-term tightening but the forward-looking Taylor rule indicating slightly looser policy. We've written a lot about the fiscal-inflation trade-off in Japan. Very simply, high inflation creates fiscal space. It flatters the nominal GDP denominator, brings debt on a downward path, allows a country to run larger fiscal deficits. For a government that wants to be able to spend more on defense or energy or AI, fiscal space is important. So there's two ways of looking at it. One, genuine economic caution around ensuring the recovery is in a good place. The cost-benefit analysis For the US, one could argue that the benefit of winning the war is decreasing over time, as the longer it takes to win the war and influence the energy matrix of the Middle East, the less the bargaining power vis a vis other countries that compete for influencing the world order. At the same time, the marginal costs are increasing and convex, as the longer the war, the higher the military and political costs. For Iran, one could argue that the benefits are increasing over time, as the longer the war, the higher the deterrent effect on the US and Israel to avoid a potential next round in the future. We would think of marginal costs as U-shaped, very high at the beginning due to the economic impact of the US bombing, relatively low as the war progress as Iran can keep the Strait closed with relatively low military spending, and very high later on as the country could run out of ammunition or food. Equilibrium in the war of attrition If these costs and benefit functions were perfectly observable by all, the equilibrium would be a short war (or in fact, no war to begin with). Solving recursively, it would be clear for both parties which one is the strongest, and the weakest would capitulate in the first place, saving all the costs associated with the war. records.text: Japan Macro Watch24 April 2026 ab 3 Underlying inflation is already rising Another area that warrants close attention is inflation expectations, which the BoJ considers one of the key components of underlying inflation. It remains fresh in memory that the Tankan survey showed an increase in medium- to long-term inflation expectations among firms. Household surveys have also revealed a notable rise: the expected inflation rate five years ahead increased from 9.8% in December last year (a level that already carries an upward bias) to 10.3%, marking the highest reading since the survey began in 2004. Both the Tankan and the latest household survey do not fully incorporate the impact of the Middle East conflict due to the timing of the surveys. As a result, there is a risk that inflation expectations could rise further in the next round of surveys. Should this materialise, it would likely heighten the BoJ’s concern about being “behind the curve.” Steadily growing exports March trade statistics confirmed that real exports remained firm. Source: Citi Research Source: Citi Research Longer-Lived Implications of this Episode Even in a favorable scenario in which the United States and Iran quickly reach an agreement to end the conflict and reopen the Strait, this episode is likely to leave a longer-term imprint on global oil markets. First, the path of oil prices through the second half of this year and into 2027 will be higher than it otherwise would have been. While much of the currently lost production could come back online within weeks, some of it—including production, refining, and pipeline capacity in the Middle East—has been directly hit during the conflict. Estimates suggest that several million barrels/day could be offline for a year or longer. The upshot is likely to be a much tighter oil market during the second half of the year than we expected as the year began. Applying traditional rules of thumb, we find that such losses could push Brent prices to around $75 to $80/barrel, well above their $60 pre-conflict path (Figure 9). records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 20 New Zealand As a net energy importer, the oil price shock will exert a terms of trade decline that will lower national income and economic growth. The end result is that we forecast year average GDP growth of 1.2% this year, down from 1.8% previously. We expect the slowdown to be concentrated in Q2 with some drag in Q3. The labour market response to even slower growth will likely be to push the unemployment rate higher. We expect the 2026 year-end unemployment rate to be 5.5%, up from the previous 5.2% view. Our yearly average headline CPI forecast for 2026 is now 3.7% vs 2.9% previously. The peak quarterly CPI impact is assumed to occur in Q2 (+1.4%), reflecting the increase in prices of imported liquid fuels that will also start influencing downstream prices for CPI basket items requiring liquid fuels-based transport freight. The RBNZ is in a difficult position, entering the oil shock with a negative output gap and excess slack in the labour market. But significant slack should shield parts of domestic inflation from higher imported prices, so we continue to expect no change to the 2.25% OCR this year. Figure 26. records.text: Moderate Supply Response Outside the Middle East Our forecast of 2026 global supply ex Gulf is 1.0mb/d higher than before the Hormuz shock (Exhibit 10) with contributions from Russia (+0.4mb/d), the US (+0.3mb/d) and Kazakhstan (+0.2mb/d). We expect stable Russia liquids supply at 10.5mb/d in 2026 (vs. a decline prior) on higher oil prices and higher producer profits, but still see downside risk from drone strikes. The 0.3mb/d upgrade to 2026 US oil supply vs. pre-war projections is modest because of market expectations of a short duration of the Hormuz shock, low DUCs (drilled but uncompleted wells), negative prices for Waha natural gas associated with oil production, and shale capital discipline. Once the Strait reopens, the largest supply response will likely come from Saudi Arabia and the UAE raising production in 2026H2 above pre-war levels (Exhibit 6). In our base case, on a YoY basis, global supply falls 12.1mb/d in 2026Q2 before returning to modest growth in Q4. records.text: ocessed food inflation started to soften last month after several months of increases, and we see room for further drops, as well as for processed food pipeline pressures to continue to point to further easing. Similar to goods inflation, at this stage, we see no pipeline pressures from higher energy commodity prices. Close to the ECB baseline projections: The recent retracement of oil and (especially) natural gas prices means commodity prices are currently close to the ECB baseline from the March-26 projections. In that scenario, the ECB expected 2Q26 headline HICP at 3.1%Q and our April forecast is consistent with that projection. Looking beyond the short term, under these conditions, the risks of very significant indirect and second-round effects, as depicted in the ECB alternative scenarios, look contained. As discussed in our ECB preview of the April meeting (here), we think this is a context where the ECB will want to keep all options on the table: we expect it will be on hold in April and think a hike in June is possible. We note, though, that the high volatility in energy prices renders our conviction in the baseline unusually low. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 16 Germany Germany has significant exposures to energy prices: utility and transport fuel bills are already high by European standards and pose competitiveness issues for the country’s manufacturing base; that the latter produces internal combustion engine cars reinforces this vulnerability. As expected, the government has reacted with temporary excise tax cuts and other measures, as well as ‘industrial electricity price’ programme (to run through 2028) to help with competitiveness problems. France France arguably has fewer vulnerabilities than Germany but limited fiscal space to absorb shocks of any kind. With nuclear produced electricity often sold at significant mark-up at market prices, a discussion about energy pricing, which reflects the marginal production cost rather than the average one, has gained traction. With Presidential elections approaching, a promise to withdraw from the European electricity market could be politically appealing but would likely create significant friction with the EU Commission. Italy We shaved 0.2pp off 2026 growth and added 1.2pp to inflation on the back of the energy shock last month and we stick to that view. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Financial Conditions: The market is doing the Fed's work so far Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 30bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the April 7 ceasefire announcement, however, financial conditions have eased by 42bps. This March tightening reversed all of the easing seen earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings, and was primarily driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. The net tightening since February 28 has been driven mainly by higher 10-year U.S. Treasury yields and dollar appreciation, with higher oil prices playing a secondary role. Exhibit 10:

As we have consistently emphasized, volatility is the most mean- reverting of all interest rate assets and will normalize over time—however, we expect this to materialize at an elevated level relative to pre-conflict norms, reflecting a structurally higher uncertainty premium around both the ECB path and the durability of the ceasefire. The normalization is therefore more likely to be gradual and partial than a clean convergence back to February averages. That said, we have pushed back our ECB hike forecast in response to the central bank's tone and lack of urgency, which should mechanically reduce near-term policy-path uncertainty and should cap the upside in implieds; the counterweight is that the overall uncertainty regime remains elevated, which argues for an ongoing risk premium embedded in the volatility surface. In terms of implementation, we make two key points. First, we prefer fading vol richness selectively and only in the 10Y+ sector. The 10Y+ sector has exhibited a lower beta to yields and to headline-driven repricing, a pattern we expect to persist given that the front end retains greater sensitivity to ECB-path surprises. The FX-Rates Relationship in an Energy Shock Risk and energy, not rates, have been the key drivers of FX markets recently Nominal rate differentials have explained a lower-than-usual portion of FX price action over the past two months (Exhibit 1). This is unsurprising given the scale of the spillovers to FX from energy prices and risk appetite in the wake of the conflict in the Middle East, but in our view, there are other factors driving this result as well. First, while rates markets have seen exceptionally large moves throughout the shock, the moves across G10 markets have generally been directionally uniform in response to the ebb and flow in energy prices. Relative to the front end as well, Bunds continue to trade less than 1-sigma cheap, in a break from the trend since the announcement of the German fiscal stimulus. Overall, the outlook for Bunds remains conditional on a credible de-escalation of the conflict (or lack thereof). For a sustainable break of 3%+ yields to realise, front-end pricing would need to increase further into a protracted hiking cycle. On the other hand, the guessing game regarding when (not if) the ECB sees enough evidence of inflationary pressures to adjust policy rates higher leaves limited scope for a rally back to the pre-war levels. Looking through the lens of real and HICP forwards, an interesting picture emerges. The energy price shock has bull-flattened the HICP forward curve, with 1y1y HICP moving higher versus the belly of the curve, resulting in a U-shaped term structure. However, the real term structure has remained upward sloping. This effectively results in a situation where belly HICP forwards are anchored around 2%, but similar-maturity real rate forwards are higher and still in restrictive territory. Given the nature of the shock and the expect negative effect of growth, this makes the belly of the real rate curve look cheaper than before the war. Statement: risk of “two-sided risks” The big question around the FOMC statement is whether it will indicate that risks to the policy path are two-sided. One way to do this would be to change the reference to “additional adjustments” to the policy rate in the forward guidance language to “any adjustments” or simply “adjustments”. This would indicate that the next move wouldn’t necessarily be in the same direction as the previous one. Per the minutes, “some participants judged that there was a strong case for” making such a change in the March statement. These hawks are likely to be just as vocal, and possibly more emboldened by the labor data, at the April meeting. So it’s a close call, but we think the majority of the committee would prefer to leave the forward guidance language unchanged. We do expect one change to the statement. Our strategists also believe corporates in Japan today are more sensitive to import prices, meaning companies will likely pass-through energy costs to consumers with limited profit margin deterioration (Figure 13). On the other hand, further escalation would increase the risk of the price shock becoming permanent, more like the 2022 shock. Hence, while we remain optimistic on the outlook, we prefer to be long in markets more exposed to the AI theme and less so to oil imports and wait for a full resolution before considering a long in Japan. On balance, they expect the euro area fiscal stance to turn mildly expansionary in 2026, with the general government deficit rising to 3.6% of GDP , from 3.1% of GDP in 2025. Clearly, as things stand, the scale of the fiscal support needed remains considerably smaller than in the previous energy crisis, even considering Italy and Germany, which are the most exposed. Naturally, this fiscal slippage and the negative growth shock create a challenging mix for debt sustainability dynamics, especially when countries are refinancing themselves at considerably higher rates relative to the cost of the stock of debt outstanding ( Figure 17). However, as we have seen time and again, for challenging debt dynamics to create a market event, there needs to be a catalyst. Historically, this catalyst has been a flare-up in political uncertainty, as in France in 2024 and 2025 and Italy in 2018. Should this energy shock linger and create a protracted challenge to economic fundamentals, spreads in countries that go to polls next year (Italy, France) could come under pressure. But this is not today's problem. records.text: United States: Inflation Markets Shelter from the geopolitical storm Outside of the next few months, the US inflation market has not dramatically shifted the priced monthly path since the Iran war started. Recent data on new lease rent growth emphasizes downside risks to our baseline, which itself already assumed further rent disinflation. A picture is worth 1000 words (or a few basis points) Headlines and noise related to the war in Iran remain top of mind, but rather than indulge in armchair geopolitical expertise, in which we have little edge, we want to instead make a more direct point. Despite the Iran war having clearly spread wider and persisted longer than the market initially assumed, the US inflation market is still pricing in a short-lived price- level shock, and not a meaningfully different inflation path beyond the next couple months. We can see this in a pure form by comparing the fixings-implied NSA m/m path from month-end in February (right before the Iran war started) to today's ( Figure 1). FIGURE 1. Elsewhere, we expect staff to zoom in on the likely slowdown in labour supply growth this year, as well as on the supply chain disruptions stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. records.text: April BoC Preview: Holding Steady The BoC remained on hold in March, reflecting a balance between weak economic data and concerns that higher energy prices could push up inflation. We expect that these same concerns will lead to another hold at this week’s meeting (decision at 9:45am ET on Wednesday, April 29). Intermeeting economic data left the data dashboard little changed relative to March (Exhibit 1). Headline inflation rose sharply on higher energy prices in March, but core inflation surprised to the downside and underlying inflation measures remained soft (CPI-Median and CPI-Trim avg at +2.3 yoy, +1.6% 3ma). And while the labor market appears to be stabilizing, the unemployment rate remains well above its historical average. The Q1 BoC surveys similarly did not signal a notable change in the outlook, with the inflation discussion appearing benign. Firms’ expectations of wage growth and output price growth declined ahead of the war in the Middle East, while consumers’ near-term inflation expectations moved sideways and long-term expectations edged down. In follow-up surveys after the start of the war in Iran, businesses raised their inflation expectations, but “many” expressed concerns about their ability to pass on higher costs. Consumers expected the war to raise prices but indicated that their inflation expectations would be highly contingent on the duration of the conflict. Against this backdrop, we expect the BoC will remain firmly on hold at this week’s meeting. O

Given the purely supply shock nature of the conflict, pricing more rate hike premium for 2026 is likely to bring increased probability of reversal of these hikes in 2027 (ie, Z6Z7 flatter). Equally, a fully credible de-escalation that leads oil flows to improve and crude prices to take another leg lower should reduce the hikes priced in Z6. However, given that it will take time fully to understand the inflation and growth effect of this conflict, the market is unlikely to reduce the pricing of ECB rate hikes to 0bp. Instead, Z6 pricing could shift from the current 2-3 hikes to 1-2 hikes. While such a bullish repricing would steepen that curve, it would unlikely be enough to push it into positive territory, given that the market would still likely price some probability of an unwind in 2027. One scenario where this slope could turn positive is if the ECB continues to wait for evidence on inflationary pressures from second-round effects and the market pushes out some of the rate hike pricing from 2026 into 2027. However, it would take time for this scenario to play out and is likely not a shift the market can make in H1 this year. records.text: Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder 24 April 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material Private credit: Growing pains In the absence of increased commercial bank lending, private credit has provided a boost to consumer and business growth. Given the opacity of this market, investor unease has the potential to spread rapidly . In that vein, liquidity and credit deterioration worries have both been rising. In this paper, we separate these 2-drivers of volatility through a lens of public and private market data, media sentiment and bottom-up asset proxies. It appears the current environment is experiencing a liquidity adjustment rather than showing signs of credit impairment . While the cycle is indeed mature , unless we see a deterioration of ample systemwide liquidity, any significant deterioration looks well contained for now. To produce next week’s GDP estimate, national statistical institutes will thus have to form a view on the unobserved March data (on the basis of higher-frequency data and surveys), with any surprises relative to those predictions possibly resulting in revisions to estimated GDP in subsequent readings. The very early hard data points for March, such as Spanish social security employment (+0.4%mom) and German truck toll mileage (-0.3%), have not sent a strong signal yet. March surveys generally pointed to a decline in consumer confidence which appears to have weighed on soft services indicators (notably in last month’s PMIs), while manufacturing activity was reportedly supported by order frontloading and strategic stock-building. Simply put, the exercise aims to understand if the asset price changes during the escalation and de- escalation phases relative to the changes in oil prices over the same period have been comparable. If a specific asset's reaction to changes in oil prices was the same on the way up as on the way down, it will lie on the 45-degree line. It appears that majority of the instruments considered in this analysis have shown larger moves relative to the changes in Brent in the de-escalation phase (lower oil prices) versus the escalation phase. Specifically, 1y1y EUR vol appears as an outlier in this framework, followed by BTP-Bunds, as their reaction to the decline in oil price is almost as twice as large as the increase in oil prices during the escalation phase. Similarly, 1y1y HICPx appears as an outlier on the other side of the 45-degree line, signaling very limited reaction to oil price declines compared with oil price increases. While market positioning and other initial conditions at the onset of the war likely also contributed to these moves compared with the evolution of Brent prices, the framework does provide a neat snapshot for understanding relative price shifts. All else equal (and purely through the lens of this vanilla approach), BTP-Bunds and 1y1y vol seem to have asymmetry to the upside should the war escalate, whereas 1y1y HICPx appears rich should there be a further de-escalation and, hence, a decline in oil prices. 23 Apr

Contemporaneous rules are straightforward - across the board, these would be consistent with near-term hikes, we would assume. The forward-looking Taylor rules are more nuanced. In the upside scenario, we assume these would be signalling at least one hike in the near term (by year-end), with cuts in the second part of the forecast horizon. Likewise, in the downside scenario, forward-looking rules ought to be consistent with cuts by year-end. In the base case, we think the very near term would be consistent with a hold, with mildly higher rates through 2027, and lower through 2028 and 2029. Various inflation and output gap forecasts could be utilised to explain the policy trade- offs. Following the market-implied Bank Rate path in the central scenario means a faster return to target than in the forward-looking Taylor scenario, albeit with a bigger output gap. Moreover, to the extent that higher inflationary pressures keep the BCB on a more cautious easing path (our economists now expect a 25bp cut at next week’s meeting), the carry component of total returns will remain even more supported, and FX longs will screen as more attractive than rates receivers. With this in mind, we think that the main near-term risk to BRL returns is a reversal of the recent risk recovery. In our view, expressing BRL longs in a more risk-neutral format, for instance with CLP funding, would be an effective way of adding resilience. Further out, we expect risks to BRL spot performance to shift from ‘global’ to ‘local’ as the October Presidential election nears. Earlier in the year, we argued that election risks were asymmetric towards BRL appreciation. But, after the YTD rally, we see risks as more two-sided; and higher volatility around the election will also lead to an erosion of carry-to-vol ratios. records.text: market functioning The escalation of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East triggered a sharp rise in macro volatility, with rate, oil, and equity volatility rising in March. Risk assets sold off, albeit modestly, while Treasury yields increased as investors pared back rate cut expectations for 2026 amid inflation concerns. Despite the increase in volatility, Treasury market functioning and liquidity conditions were resilient. There were few signs of intermediation constraints across relative value metrics. Progress towards a ceasefire and optimism about a peace deal have helped stabilize market conditions. Equities have retraced earlier losses and are now trading at all-time highs, and Treasury yields have fallen from March peaks. Volatility indicators have largely declined below pre-war levels. Overall, the Treasury market passed the “stress test” posed by recent events. Gradual improvements from the Treasury and regulators over the years have helped keep market functioning stable, especially during periods of stress. Treasury liquidity has been less susceptible to periods of vol shocks ( Figure 1). Buybacks introduced in 2024 have given dealers an avenue to offload less liquid off-the-runs, improving secondary market liquidity. records.text: 1 Insights Information Classification: General Global Equity Strategy Daniel Gerard US Equities: Worst behind us or pain ahead? Once again, markets had a wild first quarter driven by geopolitical risk, and once again , investors are asking if this liquidity driven bull market that’s lasted years has finally met its match. Although many are asking the question given building risks, investors aren’t panicking, nor are they shifting to the traditional defensive playbook. They reduced their risk appetite, but even now, as questions remain as to the durability of a cease fire in Iran, cautious optimism remains. Are investors justified in their wait and watch mode, or just way too complacent and setting up for pain? Q1’25 taught markets a key lesson; that unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty became a dull axe to risk appetite once the extent of the action became a known factor. The experience of 2025 is likely one of the reasons why there is such a large disconnect between headline risk and a more serious market impact. Many investors who had bought into a story of a global shakeup and US decline due to the policy error of tariffs were left puzzled when expectations turned to be much worse than the impact. US earnin gs didn’t collapse, spending wasn’t torpedoed, and the hope of the European recovery remained a hope. Given energy and food prices are likely to rise, the BoE would be particularly sensitive to the impact of these categories on inflation expectations. The jump in PMI output prices is likely to concern the MPC as it increases risks of firms passing on cost increases. At the same time, financial conditions have tightened, the labour market/growth is weak and could worsen, which would imply risks of significant second round effects are less than in 2022 and would reduce the need for an aggressive response. Having said that, stronger than expected growth and lower unemployment rate (even if due to fall in participation) heading into the conflict should provide a better starting point for the economy/labour market. The acceleration in April PMIs though tentative should also reduce some growth concerns and allow the BoE to focus on price pressures. We expect two hikes in 2026 but it’s a close call Given our expectation of higher energy prices persisting through the year, we expect two hikes in June and July, with risks of one, as an insurance to guard against second round effects but it’s a close call. We then expect three quarterly cuts from Q2 2027 to 3.5%, with risks of 3.25% and earlier cuts.

GSEs updated its Selling Guide to permit current use of VantageScore 4.0 and future use of FICO 10T. The rollout is structured as a limited pilot with approved lenders who can choose between Classic FICO or VantageScore 4.0 through tri- merge credit reports. Non-participating lenders must continue using Classic FICO exclusively. Fannie Mae also committed to publishing expanded historical credit score data this summer. VantageScore 4.0 incorporates trended credit data and alternative data sources— including rental, utility, and telecommunications payment histories—to enhance creditworthiness assessment. Compared to Classic FICO, VS4 demonstrates marginal predictive improvement and captures a higher proportion of defaults in the riskiest decile. The inclusion of non-traditional credit repayment tradelines is designed to expand credit access for borrowers with thin or limited traditional credit files. Analysis of GSE loan data from 2013 through 2023 reveals that VantageScore 4.0 scores average 5-15 points higher than Classic FICO, with larger divergences observed during the COVID period when absolute borrower scores were elevated (Figure 1). March’s CPI Inflation reached 3.4%MoM and has shown 10 consecutive months of increase. The conflict in the Middle East, if short-lived, would likely be limited to disruptive relative price dynamics. However, the current situation is vulnerable to external shocks, as a prolonged conflict in the Middle East could raise global interest rates and trigger capital outflows, spotlighting risks of low reserves and relatively illiquid capital markets. In the medium term, a potential shift in exports toward mining and energy risks creating the so-called "Dutch Disease" phenomenon where currency appreciation and high inflation render other export sectors uncompetitive. Chile Chile enters 2Q26 with stable macro conditions, but momentum constrained by politics and renewed inflation noise. Activity remains modest and uneven: external demand and services exports are providing support, but labor market softness and hesitant private investment continue to cap upside. Looking ahead, while our base case is for rates to remain on hold into 2027, we see a growing tail risk that policymakers could consider hiking in the coming months if the Hormuz closure persists and US labor data remains resilient. Our criterion for a rate hike is a combination of unemployment falling toward 4% (a level at which wage-price amplification becomes easier to envision) and long-term inflation expectations increasing in consumer surveys similar to the 2025 rise. Labor data from both the BLS and ADP suggests that hiring is picking up and is above current estimates of labor force growth, posing a risk that the unemployment rate may decline in coming months. We will take careful note in Chair Powell’s press conference of the extent to which he foams the runway for hikes should this fact pattern of declining unemployment and rising inflation come to pass. records.text: INR: Falling fast and slow. As the energy shock from the Iran conflict and the Strait n of Hormuz blockade has dragged on, the Rupee has continued to trade on the back foot. The ceasefire and the associated compression in the upside energy tail probably played a role in the RBI partially easing restrictions on currency derivative transactions by banks, and as a consequence, the market should be able to focus again on macro and currency fundamentals. In that regard, on the positive side, the currency is (very) modestly undervalued on a real trade-weighted basis, and the economy has demonstrated impressive resilience in the early part of this shock, with data surprising to the upside relative to the demand destruction we were factoring in. However, as long as the energy blockage persists, we think that the negatives outweigh the positives. The shock is still likely to leave an imprint on the BoP data with both higher-for-longer energy import prices and lower remittances from the middle-east; we expect limited capital inflows both given the negative terms-of-trade shock and a much more constructive outlook for equity earnings in North Asia and LatAm within EM; and even in the event of further de-escalation, we would expect policy authorities to focus on rebuilding reserves (and unwinding the short forward book) rather than encouraging currency appreciation. records.text: my. Consumer confidence, particularly in the US, played a key role in sustaining growth despite a stalling labor market. Given a baseline of continued growth in the US near 2% with stable job creation and core inflation around 3%, the Fed is unlikely to ease policy in 2026. Labor markets are expected to remain stable, with US job growth normalizing to roughly 100,000–125,000 per month. Inflation, which had previously shown signs of differentiation across regions, is expected to move higher globally due to elevated energy costs and additional supply-side pressures. Amidst this backdrop, central banks globally are likely to remain patient in the face of energy-driven inflation increases, avoiding premature tightening. Looking further ahead, the policy conversation may shift toward potential tightening in 2027 if labor markets remain firm and inflation proves persistent. With global oil supply buffers drawing down continuously, the clock is ticking. Global oil supply currently faces a shortfall of ~13mn barrels per day against demand of ~102mn barrels per day, exceeding the demand shock experienced during the peak of the COVID-19 crisis of ~7mn barrels per day. As we have consistent- ly highlighted, Buxl spreads are primarily driven by the 10s/30s swap curve, with the empir- ical relationship between the two being stable and well-defined (Figure 21. . . a s a l o w - b e t a p r o x y t o o u r 1 0 s / 3 0 s s w a p c u r v e s t e e p e n i n g v i e w ). The medium- term steepening bias on 10s/30s is itself supported by multiple factors: an expected gradual decline in 1Yx1Y €STR yields from current levels as the ECB’s urgency to hike fades, a continued normalization of implied volatility as the geopolitical risk premium dissipates at the margin, and persistent structural hedging flows from Dutch pension fund transitions and Solvency II-related demand that provide a durable bid for long-end duration. The Bund/ Buxl spread curve steepener therefore remains our preferred way to hold this view—offer- ing a lower-beta, cleaner expression of long-end steepening without the full convexity risk of an outright Buxl widener.
