Treasury liquidity conditions were resilient during the March stress episode (see here), with few signs of impaired market functioning despite the sharp rise in volatility across oil, equities, and rates. Metrics such a spline errors, futures-cash basis, and funding spreads were stable. While swap spreads tightened, the move was orderly and did not exhibit the forced deleveraging or stop-outs seen during last April's post-Liberation day move. Relative to past stress events, Treasury liquidity has less sensitive to vol shocks in recent years. While longer-tenor swap spreads have recovered, they are still below pre-war levels and we believe this reflects concerns about fiscal deterioration. The 20y point cheapens when vol spikes and reverses as conditions normalizes. That said, the 20y sector still looks cheap on the 10s20s30s ASW fly when controlling for rate volatility ( Figure 8). We see scope for the 20y leg to richen back towards the ~20bp range and recommend being long the 10s20s30s ASW fly (1:2:1, entry: 25.5bp). 23 April 2026 26 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Holding pattern

records.text: Japan Macro Watch24 April 2026 ab 2 BoJ likely to adopt wait-and-see stance We continue to expect that the Bank of Japan will keep its policy rate unchanged at the current level of 0.75% at the Monetary Policy Meeting scheduled for the 28th next week. Media reports released this week have also pointed to an unchanged policy stance, lending support to our view. According to the OIS market, the probability priced in for a rate hike is also only around 5%, making it unlikely that the BoJ would deliberately deliver a surprise hike that could disrupt markets. At the meeting, the BoJ should also release updated economic and inflation outlooks. We expect a downward revision to the economic outlook, alongside a significant upward revision to the inflation forecast. The decision to keep the policy rate unchanged is likely driven by the desire to assess developments in the Middle East. As a result, the timing of the next rate hike—now shifted from April—has narrowed to June or July as the key focal point. Given that the pause is intended to allow time to gauge geopolitical risks in the Middle East, we believe it is unlikely that Governor Ueda will clearly signal the timing of the next rate hike at the post-meeting press conference. At present, both UBS and many BoJ watchers expect the next rate hike to take place in June. Judging by intraday moves ( Figure 9), the March meeting outcome was ultimately perceived as slightly more dovish than markets had been positioned for, though this should be seen against the backdrop of a sharp intraday sell‑off following the BoE meeting earlier on the same day, which arguably lowered the bar for a dovish surprise. In this regard, Figure 8 compares current market pricing with that prevailing on the day before the March meeting. If current pricing were to hold, the market would enter the next meeting priced slightly more hawkishly than it was in March: more than 20bp worth of hikes by the June meeting and c.60bp by the end of 2026. Bearing in mind the pricing backdrop, a relatively hawkish scenario would lead the ECB to signal that, as the most recent tightening episode has shown, policy action can be forceful, entailing jumbo and potentially back‑to‑back rate hikes, if required. Lagarde could also stress during the press conference that even under the baseline scenario, the ECB’s projection for inflation returning to the 2% target by 2027 was already conditional on a yield curve pricing close to two 25bp hikes by the end of this year, though this would still be line with current pricing. More generally, downplaying growth risks while emphasising the economy’s resilience to recent shocks, persistently elevated services inflation, and the fragility of inflation expectations would be perceived as hawkish at the margin. 23 April 2026 33 Bar

records.text: 6 23 April 2026 Geopolitics has entered a fundamentally different era of re-armament, supply chain resilience, and shifting alliances, with markets and the politicians/ intelligentsia holding sharply divergent near-term views. Panelists do not expect the post-WW2 world order to return; instead, a new equilibrium is to be found amid militarization, China’s entrenched presence across global supply chains, and a transactional US-China relationship. In this new world order, resilience and self-reliance are important and J.P. Morgan’s Security and Resiliency Initiative (SRI) is one acknowledgment of this different looking world. That said, Western alliances also remain essential, even as the current US administration’s focus remains on the Western hemisphere. records.text: 6 Europe Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 But they could still look through it News on the Iran war over the past few days has raised the question of whether, with energy prices where they are today, the ECB could choose to look through the shock and not hike at all. We would not go that far – at least not yet. As argued above, with energy prices not far from baseline, surprises would be needed for the ECB to look through the shock. That said, there is still a non-negligible possibility that the ECB could do that or potentially wait a little longer to move. Non-linear effects on economic activity could be one such surprise. Lower energy prices than in the baseline could be another. And even with energy prices broadly in line with the baseline, they still might not hike – composition matters (Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4). If gas prices continue to surprise on the downside, as they have so far, that could be another rationale for looking through the shock if this led the ECB to question its inflation forecast for 2028. Less of a fiscal response than assumed could do the trick, too. In other words, while a “look-through” is far from being our baseline, it is also far from being ruled out. And at this point, the likelihood of the ECB looking through the shock is higher, to us, than that of it hiking by more than 50bp.

The Q1 2026 inflation surprise: Inflation surprised to the upside in the first quarter of 2026, with headline CPI hitting 4.1% year-on-year in March, well above the central bank’s 3.6% expectation (see Fig 1). The spikes were strongest in February and March, when CPI prints beat consensus forecasts and showed broader-based pressure than expected. Key drivers included: ▪ reversal of food-deflation trends, ▪ re-acceleration of regulated prices, especially fuels, ▪ sticky services inflation, barely responding to earlier monetary tightening, and ▪ higher airline fares, defying the usual early-year seasonal dip. The surprise is not due to a single component. It reflects a mix of cyclical and cost-driven shocks that raise inflation’s persistence. Diffusion indices and all five of the central bank’s core measures have also risen, indicating that price pressure is spreading across the CPI basket rather than staying concentrated. KEY MESSAGES We increased our Brazil-inflation outlook to 5.2% in 2026 from 4.3% earlier and 4.4% in 2027 from 4.0% previously. The upward shift reflects a Q1 surprise, a renewed rise in food prices and services inflation that stays stubbornly high. Higher energy and logistics costs, volatile global commodity markets and fertilizer-supply concerns keep inflation – especially food-price – pressure alive, while the Middle East conflict adds a medium-term supply- side risks. A third legacy of this episode is increased incentives for countries to become more energy independent. Such efforts could take several forms. First, countries are likely to focus more intensively on developing their available energy reserves. This could include gas and oil reserves, but it may also mean increased production and consumption of coal (Figure 11).3 Second, both countries and firms are likely to take steps to expand their oil inventories, which should provide increased buffers to ride through temporary shocks (Figure 12). This would parallel countries’ efforts after the GFC to accumulate FX reserves to “self-insure” and reduce their vulnerability to financial shocks. Third, policymakers could also focus on the demand side of the energy market, potentially including intensified emphasis on reducing usage and increasing efficiency. Fourth, this episode may increase the attractiveness of non- petroleum sources of energy including nuclear power and renewables. 2 Our estimates put this cost at roughly several dollars per barrel. 3 For the United States, this could take the form of increasing its refinery capacity to better match the types of oil that the country is currently producing. 50 60 70 80 90 100 110

The market’s willingness to “look through” adverse scenarios and geopolitical risk isn’t purely complacency. Outside the AI narrative, macro resilience, policy discipline and demand for diversification continue to underpin risk assets. • Economies have withstood stress tests, but scenario analysis is now the norm.DM and EM economies have outperformed expectations despite a series of shocks since COVID. Scenario analysis is now the norm, including with the IMF and major central banks, such as the ECB. Policymakers and business leaders are mapping the range of plausible paths and accepting that uncertainty is high, which is reflected with the inclusion of adverse scenarios and subsequent contingency plans. • Central banks have acted prudently despite competing pressures. For Europe and EM economies, inflation was close to target before the Iran conflict. Our economics team now forecast ECB hikes in June and September (vs. April and July) and one BoE hike in June. Meanwhile, the BoJ has signaled a hawkish hold. The Fed is seen as effectively on hold, and the point was made that the FOMC operates on a one-person, one-vote basis. • Fundamentals are strong outside of the US. EM is not facing immediate risks from balance of payments or debt vulnerabilities. Japan The inward migration of JGB underperformance. The BoJ’s more patient policy n stance has seen longer-term JGBs act as the main pressure release valve amid sustained inflation risks. But while 30s had borne the brunt of the underperformance throughout last year and early on this year, the last few months have seen the torch passed from 30s into 10s, with 30y yields sticky (albeit at higher levels) even as 10y yields have reached new cycle highs. Our JGB curve models now suggest that the 10s30s slope is very close to fair value (while 2s5s and 5s10s segments now look clearly steep; Exhibit 10)—to some extent that could reflect a healthier supply/demand dynamic at the long end following issuance adjustments and what appears to have been a stabilization in lifer demand following a period of net selling in the long end. But as we have argued in the past, we ultimately do not think that bear steepening is a sustainable equilibrium and think it is reasonable to expect additional underperformance to shift further in on the curve over time. It is not clear that next week’s BoJ meeting should provide a catalyst to a sharp shift in yields or dynamics along the curve given that the market has priced very low risks of a hike in April. Inflation jumped to 3.3% in March as expected, and despite slightly weaker core, services inflation rose to 4.5% (somewhat driven by airfares). PMIs bounced back in April, showing renewed growth momentum and improving employment, but it’s too early to make strong conclusions, as some of this reflects a short-term boost to secure purchases ahead of price rises. But price pressures dominated – input costs rose at the fastest pace since November 2022 and output price inflation was the highest since February 2023. The big acceleration in input and output prices is concerning and would give weight to the arguments of the hawks for the MPC to focus more decisively on price concerns.

Markets have remained risk-on this week, with the Nikkei 225 topping 60,000 for the first time. Tensions remain in the Strait of Hormuz, but markets price in a world after the conflict has ended. Nevertheless, momentum dominates and market movements are not necessarily consistent. Energy prices are still high and logistics bottlenecks remain, so ongoing caution is needed. Pricing of a rate hike at next week’s BoJ MPM has receded in the interest rate market. The BoJ is seen as certain to leave policy unchanged, so the focus has shifted to how strongly it will signal a rate hike at the June meeting. The BoJ is widely expected to raise its outlook for prices and lower its outlook for growth, but we do not think that the Bank itself will be particularly confident in its forecasts. This is particularly the case for the growth rate, and we think it will take more time to gauge the impact on the real economy of the situation in the Middle East. Even so, the policy rate is at a very accommodative level, and there is significant wariness about the BoJ possibly falling behind the curve if inflation accelerates. The average Total Fertility Rate (TFR) dropped from around 6.0 births per woman in the 1960s to an estimated 1.87 by 2025, well below the replacement level of 2.1. Japan and Korea are aging the fastest, followed by China and Thailand, while India and Indonesia continue to benefit from a longer window of demographic dividends. That said, we believe the demographic drag can be at least partially offset by continued gains in human capital, AI adoption, and more effective retirement‑system management. Even with fewer births, gains in health condition, increased longevity, and technology‑enabled life quality boost would imply a smaller but more capable workforce in the future. We have maintained that n the ramifications of the conflict in the Middle East will affect economic data, and FX returns, even after peak uncertainty. Higher energy prices and product shortages are rearranging global current account balances and dampening growth momentum, and relative FX returns are increasingly reflecting this differentiation. We have revised our global growth forecasts lower, with smaller revisions in the US and other energy-insulated economies. Our economists are now well below consensus in APAC ex-China, and marginally below consensus in the Euro area, with a widening gap to the US, and our 3-month FX forecasts reflect this with broad Dollar depreciation delayed. However, we must admit that, after a much longer-than-expected disruption to energy flows, the impact so far looks much less conspicuous than what we would have expected at the start of the conflict, perhaps reflecting greater reliance on accumulated inventories so impacts may be delayed. If anything, recent data have underscored the downside risks to shelter inflation, with the last several ZORI releases coming in below 10bp m/m (and the single- family ZORI negative m/m in March 2026). In essence, the latest realized ZORI prints point to a real risk of rent disinflation beyond our baseline assumption of 2.5% by end-2026, and that if that occurs, even reasonably bullish forecasts for other components still translate to a lower CPI path of about 2% versus the 2.5% priced into 1y1y inflation space. If the bearish signal from new rents is real, in inflation markets, we see space for 1y1y to underperform on the curve and continue to recommend 1y1y vs 5y5y CPI swap curve steepeners (see the inflation section for details). The bottom line is that the economy is settling into a lower equilibrium of activity and labor markets and inflation excluding tariffs is heading in the right direction with 2% not as far out of sight as is commonly perceived. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 33 UK While the MPC likely remain split, we expect the majority to be patient in assessing the inflationary consequences of the conflict in the Middle East with a bias to look- through. That seems to be the message coming from Governor Bailey of late, emphasising that the inflation remit should be met while limiting the impact on jobs and growth. Moreover, a decision to hold is already hawkish with policy rates still at a restrictive level. The front-end has already reverted to more sensible level following the positioning washout early in the conflict. We remain bullish, but more for the medium-term than the near-term. For the long-end, our yield forecasts are little changed this month (following the bearish reappraisal last month) and we continue to pencil in mildly bullish forecast of 4.5% for 10yr gilt yields in 4Q26. The potential to rally has been curtailed by the shift in the BoE outlook (from cuts to a hold for 2026 in our base case), especially with political risk (from market concerns over the longevity of the Starmer/Reeves leadership) and fiscal risk (on the funding for defence spending) back in the spotlight. These risks may keep up steepening pressure on 10s30s, especially around the known event risks of the 7 May local elections and then the all-important autumn Budget. records.text: M Idea 2 Policy Decision: Too Early to Decide European Economics Team Hold in April: We expect the ECB to remain on hold next week. We have long thought that April was an unlikely moment for the ECB to change its monetary policy stance (see here). Given the lack of data on the real side of the economy, volatility in oil and gas markets, and uncertainty around developments in the Middle East conflict, it is simply too early for the ECB to act. Meanwhile, financial conditions have tightened and done some of the work for the ECB (see here). President Lagarde reinforced our thinking on Monday, underlining that more information is needed, echoing Philip Lane's remarks that "it's too early to have anything too decisive". We expect the ECB to view its best course of action in April as adopting a 'wait and see' approach. And Council members on record over the past days were of the same view (Kazaks, Müller). The recent fall in energy prices certainly helps in the discussion, as it puts a question mark over the general case for rate hikes (see Dolenc, and our discussion below). Labor market: stabilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse. However, the shock from the Iran War to our GDP trajectory should imply slower job growth. But with GDP still close to trend, we wouldn't expect the labor market to roll over. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 40k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate at 4.5% in 2Q26 and then dropping to 4.4% by 4Q26 and 4.3% by 4Q27. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but delayed to Sep-Oct • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at its Mar meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed emphasized that the economic implications of the Iran war are uncertain. Powell’s comments discussed at length the ongoing inflation overshoot and upside risks to inflation, but barely discussed downside risks to the labor market. records.text: en increases In response to rising crude oil prices amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, Japan's government has reinstated gasoline subsidies. In addition, with electricity and gas bills expected to rise from June, the government is also likely to reinstate electricity and gas bill subsidies through the summer. While these measures should help limit the near‑term impact on domestic growth and inflation, they come at the cost of higher fiscal burdens. The government plans to fund the subsidies using contingency reserves of up to ¥2.1tn, however, maintaining them at this scale increases the risk that the funds will run out before summer. This increases the likelihood of a first supplementary budget ahead of summer (around June-July). Indonesia: BI delivered a hold; near term focus remains on IDR stability In Indonesia, BI kept the policy rate unchanged at 4.75%, as widely expected, citing the need to facilitate "stronger" IDR. Further monetary policy tightening moves - including adjustment to policy rate - were not ruled out. The central bank also announced that some primary dealers would be allowed to sell in offshore NDFs, aimed at better aligning offshore NDF pricing with onshore FX market. We see policy rate unchanged for some time, with BI probably more tolerant of wider SRBI-policy rate spread than before.

A combination of Q1 upside, renewed food-price pressure and stubborn services inflation is occurring alongside risk from the Middle East conflict. We lift our Brazil-inflation outlook to 5.2% in 2026 from 4.3% earlier and 4.4% in 2027 from 4.0% previously. The shift reflects near-term shocks and a more persistent second-round drag, especially from fertilizers, global commodities and price-level inertia. We now see the Selic rate ending 2026 at 13.5% instead of the 12.5% we previously projected. The central bank now faces a harder trade-off: inflation is no longer a fleeting supply shock, and expectations have begun to drift upward through 2026–2029. Meanwhile, activity remains more resilient than expected, weakening demand-side disinflation. As a result, we now expect a more conservative easing cycle, with the Selic rate ending 2026 at 13.5%, versus 12.5% previously. This could reflect the tailwind from regulation supporting growth in this area of the balance sheet, though it may also be partly a function of commercial banks shifting the composition of their securities portfolios—the increase in USTs has been mirrored by a drop in agency MBS as a share of large bank assets. We would also note, however, that the trend contrasts with a longer running reduction in UST allocation across small banks, which were unaffected by the change to the eSLR calculation. While our baseline does not anticipate a strong surge in bank demand, we continue to expect a slightly faster pace of UST buying this year versus prior years. Reserves test the relative lows with diminished effect. Reserves averaged their n lowest levels since late January, likely dipping below $2.9 trillion intraweek, which we estimate would represent a cycle low as a share of bank assets. Despite this, funding conditions have remained notably more resilient compared to late last year, even as relative liquidity has quickly revisited similarly levels (Exhibit 3). This contrast suggests that the Fed’s reserve management purchases have been effective, and it may also indicate that banks have had sufficient time to adapt to lower reserve levels and/or that frictions in the system have diminished. Given these signals, our bias remains toward a further modest reduction in the pace of reserve management purchases (our baseline is $20bn per month).

records.text: M Idea 10 Turning to the risks that could shape the post-meeting market reaction, hawkish risks would stem from a vote split that is firmer than our 8:1 hold base case, a more hawkish lean in the individual paragraphs, firmer guidance that rising risks of second-round effects would in themselves warrant policy action, or scenarios and policy rules that place greater weight on inflation persistence. That risk would be amplified if the alternative scenarios are framed in a way that emphasises inflation overshoot, and if the individual paragraphs suggest that only limited additional evidence would be needed before the Committee tightens. In that case, we would expect market pricing to shift towards a higher probability of multiple hikes, beyond the roughly two hikes currently priced, with the trough rate also moving higher. Conversely, dovish risks would stem from a more dovish vote split than in our base case, including a unanimous hold, a more balanced lean in the individual paragraphs, or scenarios and messaging that place greater weight on weaker growth, labour-market downside and the drag from tighter financial conditions. Any scenario framing that downplays inflation persistence and gives greater prominence to the growth trade-off would likely be read as dovish. In that case, we would expect pricing to move back towards a one-hike scenario and to price in a greater degree of curve inversion from 2027 onwards. First, AI and other technological developments are looking increasingly robust and transformative. At the moment, the economic support is coming primarily through increased investment. But over time, the AI revolution seems poised to diffuse through the economy and raise productivity growth. Second, there is increased familiarity—although clearly not outright comfort—with President Trump’s operating style and policy reaction function. The administration's actions suggest a tolerance for increased market volatility, while aiming to avoid a full-scale recession. Third, the resilience narrative has gained increased traction. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Economic Outlook: Checking Where We Stand European Economics Team Close to the baseline: With times so unusual and uncertainty so high, we don't expect the ECB to publish updates to the March-26 baseline and scenarios (Exhibit 2 to Exhibit 4 ). The Council discussion is likely to focus on what we have learnt since March, with, we think, three key messages. First, the recent retracement of oil and natural gas prices (as of 20 April) means commodity prices are close to the ECB baseline of March-26. At the time of writing, the risks of very significant indirect and second round effects, as depicted in the ECB alternative scenarios, look contained. Second, we still lack the data to form a view on the actual impact of higher energy prices on the economy. Third, the scenarios published in March were depicting meaningful upside risks to inflation, with limited impact on GDP. But they also did not embrace the full spectrum of potential outcomes: supply disruptions could mean more downside risk to growth and less upside risk to inflation than envisaged. records.text: Global Economic Outlook & Strategy 23 April 2026 Citi Research 13 Select Economy Discussion North America United States The Fed has left policy rates unchanged at recent meetings as the current level of policy rates allows officials to wait and see how the situation in the Middle East and data evolve. The surge in oil prices raises upside risks to core inflation and downside risk to growth. In our base case, oil prices fall in coming months and there is limited passthrough to core inflation. This combined with further weakening in the labor market could push the Fed to cut policy rates to 2.75- 3.0% by the end of the year. GDP growth slowed in Q4 in part due to the drag from the government shutdown that will likely rebound in Q1 2026. Real consumption growth has been slower in recent quarters. We continue to expect solid growth in 2026, although with some further slowing in consumption and downside risk due to the surge in energy prices. The rise in energy prices, if sustained for many months, could weigh on GDP by a few tenths of a percentage point this year. Core PCE inflation has been sticky around 3.0%YoY while core CPI has slowed a bit more to 2.5-2.6%. Headline inflation will likely continue to be strong in the near term as energy prices have remained elevated. records.text: 4 Global Economic Weekly | 24 April 2026 US Aditya Bhave BofAS Jay-hawk swan song? • The FOMC will stay firmly on hold at its April meeting, in our view. Upside risks to inflation from the Iran war haven’t dissipated. The labor data have improved. • The big question is whether the forward guidance language in the statement will indicate that risks to policy are two-sided.
